queries: Parses attacker bytes AND does pointer/size arithmetic

ANSWERS the functions where a memory-safety bug is actually reachable.
ACT this is the CWE-190 shape: a length from the wire, a shift or a cast,
     then a copy. Review these before anything else on the risk list.
MISLEADS io counts RAW descriptor calls only; a function fed by a caller
     that did the read is just as exposed and is invisible here.
Self-recursive functions, by how much stack each level costs

ANSWERS where a deeply nested input can exhaust the C stack, and how deep
     it has to be: `frame_bytes` is the automatic storage one call declares,
     `levels_per_mb` how many nested calls fit in a megabyte of stack.
ACT every one of these needs a depth cap that is TESTED at the cap. A row
     with levels_per_mb in the hundreds overflows a 512 KB thread stack on
     input a fuzzer finds in seconds.
MISLEADS DIRECT self-recursion only: mutual recursion through two functions
     or a function pointer does not appear. frame_bytes sums every local
     the body declares -- sibling scopes share slots, so it is an upper
     bound -- and leaves out the `unsized` ones (types from headers this
     file does not define, and VLAs), so it is also a floor. Read both.
Allocates but never frees in the same function

ANSWERS where allocation ownership crosses a function boundary.
ACT each row must have a NAMED owner that frees it on EVERY path --
     including the early returns and the goto-out ladder.
MISLEADS this is a REVIEW list, not a leak list. Transferring ownership
     to the caller is the normal C idiom and looks identical here.
Files that use libc malloc AND a project allocator

ANSWERS which files split their memory across two accounting systems.
ACT pick ONE per file. A project allocator usually exists to track or cap
     usage, and a libc allocation in the same file is invisible to it.
MISLEADS a project allocator is recognised by NAME SHAPE (anything ending
     in alloc/free/strdup), so an unconventionally named one is missed and
     an unrelated `list_free` is counted. Also, mixing is sometimes right:
     tracked buffers through the wrapper, private scratch through libc.
An allocation inside a loop body

ANSWERS which loops pay the allocator once per item.
ACT hoist the allocation, or reserve capacity before the loop.
MISLEADS a realloc-grow loop is amortised O(1) and belongs here anyway;
     the count is of SITES, and one site in a hot loop beats ten cold ones.
     An allocator is recognised by NAME -- the libc ones and anything ending
     in alloc, strdup or memdup (zmalloc, xcalloc) -- so a wrapper with
     another name is missed and a non-allocating `*alloc` accessor is
     counted.
Allocates BEFORE it knows the fast path applies

ANSWERS which functions pay setup cost on inputs they then refuse.
ACT probe FIRST, allocate second. This is the classic bypass candidate.
MISLEADS an allocation before a loop is usually just the output buffer,
     which has to be allocated up front and is not a tax at all.

ANSWERS what two threads could be writing at the same time.
ACT every row needs a lock, an atomic, a thread-local, or a written proof
     that only one thread ever touches it.
MISLEADS it does not know which modules are threaded. The last column is
     the only evidence offered: how many functions in the same module use
     a concurrency primitive at all.
A switch INSIDE a loop: type dispatch paid once per element

ANSWERS where a loop re-decides the same thing on every iteration.
ACT hoist the switch out, or specialise the loop per case.
MISLEADS a bytecode interpreter's dispatch loop is exactly this shape and
     is correct by design. So is a state machine.
strlen() inside a loop: accidental O(n^2)

ANSWERS where a length is recomputed that cannot have changed.
ACT hoist it, or carry the length beside the string.
MISLEADS a strlen over a SHORT string is a few cycles, and a loop whose
     body mutates the string has to recompute it.
Functions that report failure in more than one shape

ANSWERS where a caller can plausibly check the wrong thing.
ACT a function returning both NULL and -1 is one that callers get wrong
     roughly half the time. Pick one convention per function and document
     it in the header, where the caller is actually looking.
MISLEADS returning 0 for success AND 0 as a legitimate value is the worst
     case of all and is completely invisible here.
Nothing in this tree calls these or names them

ANSWERS what might be deletable: private functions with no caller and whose
     name is never used as a value -- not passed as a callback, not stored
     in a field, not listed in a file-scope table.
ACT grep the name as a STRING before deleting anything: a name assembled by
     token pasting or looked up at run time keeps a symbol alive with no
     reference to show for it.
MISLEADS `graph-blindspots` measures how much of the call graph is unseen.
     Public symbols are excluded because a caller outside this tree cannot
     be seen at all. A function whose only caller is itself dead is NOT
     listed -- this is one layer, not a transitive sweep. The functions kept
     alive only by a table or a callback are in dispatch-table-orphan and
     fnptr-blindspot-callers.
a libc call with a shared static buffer, in a function that also touches threads

ANSWERS CERT CON33-C and MSC24-C, which clang-tidy states as a per-call
     rule and cppcheck barely states at all: `localtime`, `strerror`,
     `getenv`, `basename` and friends return a pointer into one static
     buffer. Single-threaded that is correct and cheap. In a function that
     also creates threads or takes locks it is a data race that corrupts
     the OTHER thread's result, silently, under load.
ACT use the _r form -- localtime_r, strerror_r, getpwnam_r -- or copy the
     result before releasing the lock. `patterns` names exactly which
     calls, so the fix is mechanical.
MISLEADS a function that touches threads is not necessarily called from
     more than one, and pthread_create in main() next to a getenv() at
     startup is fine. This sees categories in the same body, not the
     happens-before between them.
atoi/strtol in a function that also reads input

ANSWERS CERT ERR34-C, which flawfinder and clang-tidy report on every
     `atoi` in the tree. `atoi("42")` on a literal is fine. `atoi` on
     bytes that just came off a socket or a file returns 0 for the string
     "0" and for garbage alike, and sets no errno to distinguish them.
     The graph supplies the missing half: whether the same function also
     performs I/O.
ACT use strtol with an end pointer and check both `end` and `errno`, or
     reject the input outright. `conversions` names the exact calls;
     `returns_value` says whether the function can even report a failure
     to its caller, and a 0 there means the error has nowhere to go.
MISLEADS co-occurrence in one body is not dataflow -- a function may read
     a file and separately parse a constant. A wrapper that validates
     before calling this one makes the row correct and harmless, and that
     wrapper is not visible in the row.

ANSWERS where unbounded buffer operations are used: sprintf, strcpy,
     strcat, gets. Each can write past the end of a buffer if the input
     is larger than expected.
ACT use snprintf, strncpy (or strlcpy), strncat, fgets. Check return values.
MISLEADS a sprintf on a buffer known to be large enough is safe, but the
     graph cannot prove the buffer size.
printf with non-literal format string (CERT STR30-C)

ANSWERS where printf/fprintf/sprintf is called with a format string that is
     not a string literal, enabling format string attacks if the string
     contains user-controlled %s or %n.
ACT use printf('%s', user_string) not printf(user_string).
MISLEADS a format string from a trusted constant array is safe. The graph
     sees the call but not the argument source.

ANSWERS where a function allocates memory but has no matching free, which
     is a leak if the allocation outlives the function and is not stored.
ACT free the allocation before returning, or document ownership transfer.
MISLEADS a function that allocates and returns the pointer to the caller is
     not leaking; the caller is responsible. The graph sees alloc/free in
     the same function, not across functions.
free called more than once on same pointer (CERT MEM40-C)

ANSWERS where a function has more free calls than alloc calls, which may
     indicate a double-free if the same pointer is freed on multiple paths.
ACT track the pointer state; set to NULL after free and check before.
MISLEADS a function that frees pointers allocated in other functions has
     more frees than allocs by design. The imbalance is a signal, not proof.
Pointer dereference without null check (CERT ERR30-C)

ANSWERS where a function dereferences pointers but has no null checks,
     which means a NULL pointer will crash the program.
ACT check for NULL before dereferencing, especially after malloc/calloc.
MISLEADS a pointer known to be non-null (from a trusted source) does not
     need a check. The graph sees n_null_check but not which pointers.

ANSWERS where integer arithmetic is performed without overflow checking,
     which is UB for signed integers and wraps for unsigned.
ACT use checked arithmetic (__builtin_add_overflow) or validate inputs.
MISLEADS arithmetic on known-small constants is safe. The graph counts
     arithmetic sites but not the operand ranges.
Division by a variable the function never tests (CERT INT33-C)

ANSWERS where `/` or `%` has a plain variable as its divisor and that name
     is never compared with anything or used as a condition anywhere in the
     function. `var_divs` is every non-literal divisor, for scale.
ACT follow the divisor back to its source. A parameter needs a guard here or
     a documented precondition; a length or count needs its empty case.
MISLEADS the test is function-wide and by NAME: a guard in the caller, or on
     an alias of the same value, is invisible and the row is a false alarm.
     A divisor that is an expression (`a->n`, `f(x)`, `n + 1`) is counted in
     var_divs but never judged, so its absence here proves nothing.

ANSWERS where a switch statement has no default case, so unhandled values
     fall through silently. MISRA-C requires a default in every switch.
ACT add a default case, even if it only asserts or does nothing.
MISLEADS a switch over an exhaustive enum may not need a default, but a
     future value will be silently ignored.
Shared static variable accessed from concurrent context (CERT CON33-C)

ANSWERS where a function reads/writes a static variable and also touches
     threads, locks, or atomics, indicating potential data races.
ACT protect the shared variable with a mutex, or use thread-local storage.
MISLEADS a static variable set once at startup and only read afterward is
     safe. The graph sees co-occurrence, not the happens-before relation.
Unsafe function called inside a signal handler (CERT SIG30-C)

ANSWERS where a function that may be called as a signal handler calls
     non-async-signal-safe functions (malloc, printf, syslog).
ACT only call async-signal-safe functions inside signal handlers.
MISLEADS relies on function name matching (contains 'sig' or 'handler'),
     which is crude; a function registered via signal(2) at runtime with a
     non-obvious name is not detected.
A constant-true loop with no way out (CERT MSC53-C)

ANSWERS which `while (1)` / `for (;;)` loops contain no break, return, goto
     or call to exit/abort/longjmp anywhere in their body.
ACT confirm each one is a thread main or an event loop that is meant to run
     until the process dies -- and that something outside can stop it.
MISLEADS a worker thread and a scheduler are intentionally endless and are
     most of this list in a healthy tree. A loop left only through a called
     function that never returns (a project `fatal()`, pthread_cancel) is
     reported; a loop whose only break belongs to a nested switch is not.
Calls that drop a non-void result on the floor (CERT EXP12-C)

ANSWERS which functions return a value that callers throw away, counted per
     call SITE: `f(x);` as a whole statement, with f returning non-void.
ACT a status code that most callers ignore is an error channel nobody reads:
     check it, or change the function to void and say so. `(void)f(x);` is
     the way to mark a deliberate discard and is not counted.
MISLEADS chaining APIs return their argument for convenience (a builder, an
     sds-style append used for its side effect) and are correct to ignore.
     Sites are matched by NAME, so a function defined more than once is left
     out entirely, and a call through a pointer is never seen.
Heavily-used function-like macro that may evaluate arguments twice (CERT PRE31-C)

ANSWERS the function-like macros with the most use sites -- each use
     passes its arguments through the macro body once PER REFERENCE in
     that body, so an argument with side effects (i++, f()) is
     evaluated however many times the body names it. `uses` is the
     call-shaped reference count from call resolution.
ACT convert the top rows to static inline functions: identical
     runtime cost, but types checked, breakpoints possible, and the
     double-evaluation hazard gone.
MISLEADS a macro that references each argument exactly once is safe
     and lands here anyway (the body text is captured in macros.body
     -- read it before acting); a macro used only as a non-call token
     shows zero uses.
Functions reached through function pointers or dynamic member calls

ANSWERS where runtime target ambiguity is densest: the reads through
     `ops->`-style members and `(*fp)()` calls that a static call graph
     cannot resolve. Every one is a site whose callee is decided at runtime.
ACT audit the dispatch site: is the function-pointer slot ever written with
     something other than the one obvious initializer? If so, the edge here
     is a security boundary, not an abstraction.
MISLEADS counts CALL SITES, not distinct targets, and the brace scanner
     sees the `->`-shaped member call syntax only; a struct passed around
     and invoked through a local alias (`ops->read` copied into a local
     `fp`) shows up as the alias's direct call instead.
User-header vs system-header include ratio per file

ANSWERS which files lean almost entirely on system headers (<...>) and so
     carry little project-local coupling -- and which pull in mostly user
     headers ("..."), marking them as tightly coupled to the tree.
ACT a file at ~0%% user headers is often a portability shim; a file at
     100%% user headers that is itself widely included deserves a look for
     layering violations.
MISLEADS a `<system>` include that RESOLVES inside the tree is counted as
     user here (the analyzer treats project headers on the include path as
     internal), so the ratio is about the include SPELLING, not about where
     the file actually lives.
Mutually recursive function pairs (a calls b, b calls a)

ANSWERS the call pairs that can recurse unboundedly even though no single
     function calls itself. Each row is a 2-cycle in the resolved edge set.
ACT add a depth cap or an iteration guard on the LOWER-LEVEL member of the
     pair; the higher one is where the recursion is entered.
MISLEADS finds direct 2-cycles only. Cycles of length >= 3 (a->b->c->a)
     need a full SCC walk and do NOT appear; self-recursion is covered by
     `stack-exhaustion`, not here. Edges are name-resolved, so two functions
     that share one name are conflated.
Non-static, non-const globals: the state every translation unit shares

ANSWERS the file-scope objects without internal linkage (no `static`), so
     any translation unit that declares them extern can mutate them. Where
     `race-surface` asks which mutable globals two THREADS could clobber
     (it includes statics and singles out non-atomic ones), this asks
     which globals merely EXIST as cross-TU seams -- the ones that make a
     function untestable in isolation and a refactor a hunt through every
     declaring file.
ACT make them static and route access through one setter, or move them
     into a context struct passed explicitly.
MISLEADS the brace scanner cannot see WHICH functions write the global,
     only that it exists and is shared (`race-surface` is the same data
     through a thread-race lens); `has_init` being 0 does not prove there
     is no initializer (a forward-declared extern has none by
     construction). Config-style `extern const` tables are correctly
     excluded (is_const). The scanner records every file-scope declarator
     including function parameters of that shape, so private locals and
     pointer parameters can surface as rows; shared mutable file-scope
     objects are the rows that matter.
Headers included but none of their functions are ever called

ANSWERS the #include lines whose target file's functions have zero
     resolved callers anywhere in the tree -- the include-graph shape that
     slows rebuilds without contributing edges.
ACT drop the include if the header only carried types you no longer use;
     otherwise expect one of the covered-by-macro / config-gated cases.
MISLEADS a header used ONLY for types, macros, or constants looks dead
     here by construction (the scanner sees function calls only); a header
     whose functions are CALLED THROUGH POINTERS is also invisible. This is
     a candidate list, not a delete list.
Symbols with the largest transitive caller sets

ANSWERS which functions, if changed, can disturb the most of the tree:
     the count of DISTINCT functions that can reach this symbol through
     resolved edges at any depth.
ACT treat the top rows as API changes requiring a caller sweep: every
     row's callers are the blast zone. For a public entry point the number
     is meaningless by design -- see MISLEADS.
MISLEADS `n_transitive` counts callers THROUGH RESOLVED EDGES ONLY; a
     symbol called dynamically (function pointer) or across a name
     collision undercounts, and a widely-included header's inline helpers
     are undercounted for the same reason. The pass is an SCC fold over
     the whole graph (exact on the edges that exist); `call-chain-depth`
     in METRICS is the same table read DOWNWARD.
Struct types that span translation units via layout surface

ANSWERS the struct definitions whose shape (size, pointer fields, padding)
     makes them load-bearing across files: a struct this large or this
     pointer-heavy, defined once, is almost certainly passed between
     translation units and is a compatibility surface.
ACT treat layout changes (field reorder, pointer widening) as ABI changes
     for every included_by file; the pad columns show where the wasted
     bytes are.
MISLEADS the brace scanner cannot see WHERE a struct is instantiated; this
     ranks by DEFINED shape, not by measured usage, so a huge struct that
     never leaves its file appears here too. `exact=0` sizes (unknown field
     types) are excluded rather than guessed.
Translation units leaning on extern declarations

ANSWERS where file boundaries are load-bearing on bare extern promises:
     the count of extern-declared globals a file relies on, and the volume
     of calls resolved only because a prototype declared the callee (no
     definition in this unit).
ACT high extern + low definition density is where a symbol rename or a
     signature change breaks the tree without the compiler naming every
     victim; consider moving the shared declarations into a header.
MISLEADS n_external_calls counts calls whose callee was declared but not
     defined in the unit -- libc and POSIX calls dominate any realistic
     file, so compare DENSITY across files, not the raw number.
One function name, two different definitions across TUs

ANSWERS function names defined with >= 2 different signatures across
     translation units: UB per C99 6.2.7 (MISRA 8.3). The linker picks
     one definition and every caller of the other shape is miscompiled.
ACT pick one signature; rename or delete the other definition. The row
     names every file involved.
MISLEADS typedef-equivalent types compare different textually, so a
     benign `int foo(int)` vs `int foo(int32_t)` pair is reported;
     K&R definitions yield empty signature text and are excluded, and a
     static fn in one file plus an extern fn of the same name in another
     is NOT a link conflict yet still reads as drift here.
External-linkage functions whose callers all live in one TU

ANSWERS non-static functions whose resolved callers all sit in one
     translation unit: they should be static (MISRA 8.7, cppcheck). An
     external-linkage symbol is a coupling surface for the whole
     binary; a one-TU usage pattern says the author forgot the keyword.
ACT make it static; if fan_in is also 0, `dead-code` owns the deletion
     question instead.
MISLEADS name-based resolution undercounts callers, so a function used
     from a second TU through a macro or a function pointer reads as
     one-TU here; fnptr-dispatched users are invisible; a header inline
     absorbed elsewhere never appears. When in doubt, the compiler's
     own -Wmissing-prototypes is the tiebreaker.
Sites of dangerous process/temp APIs (CERT ENV33-C, flawfinder)

ANSWERS reachable sites of the dangerous process and temp-file API set:
     system/popen/exec for process boundaries, mktemp/tmpnam/tempnam for
     race-prone temp files, access for TOCTOU-prone checks.
ACT replace mktemp with mkstemp; interrogate every system/popen -- each
     is a command-injection review item when the argument is not a
     constant; prefer execve with an explicit argv over execl/execvp
     when the argument list is built at runtime.
MISLEADS the capture is the call scanner, independent of resolution, so
     libc calls that would otherwise classify as external still appear;
     the denylist is the fixed set above -- rand/setenv are NOT captured
     and are absent by design (their risk is caller-context, which this
     query does not model); errno-checking callers are not distinguished.

ANSWERS string literals at least 12 chars long whose text names a
     credential (password, token, api_key, secret, bearer, jwt, ...) --
     the literal that a committed secret looks like.
ACT rotate and move to a secret manager; never commit the literal.
MISLEADS a format string or test fixture containing the WORD token/pass
     reads as a candidate (the filter is the literal's own text, not its
     use); values over 200 chars are truncated at capture; a secret
     built from parts or read from an env var is invisible here. This
     is a candidate list, not a verdict.
User headers that include each other, directly or via a chain

ANSWERS user headers that include each other: the include graph is a
     DAG in any well-formed project, so a cycle means the headers are
     mutually dependent and the build order is an accident of include
     guards.
ACT break the cycle with a forward declaration or by shrinking one
     header; rows name both endpoints and the cycle length.
MISLEADS include guards make cycles harmless at compile time, so this
     is a maintainability smell, not a defect; the cycle set is
     computed at BUILD time (bounded DFS, depth cap 8) into the
     include_cycles table -- a recursive-CTE version of this query
     enumerated paths rather than cycles and never finished on large
     trees; is_relative=1 means user "..." includes, and a <...>
     include that resolves in-tree is excluded from the walk.
Casts that drop const from const-declared names (CERT EXP05-C)

ANSWERS `(T*)name` casts applied to a name declared const: the
     const-qualified promise is stripped by the cast, and any write
     through the result is UB in the caller's face.
ACT remove the cast, or drop const from the declaration if the
     function genuinely mutates (and say why).
MISLEADS the const test is against the local/param declaration in the
     SAME function: a const GLOBAL or a const from another translation
     unit is invisible here. The cast's TARGET type is not examined, so
     `(const char *)p` on a const p -- which drops nothing -- and a
     `(void *)p` handed to a hashing helper are both counted.
Functions with no caller whose name is used as a value in a body

ANSWERS functions with fan_in 0 that some function body names without
     calling: passed as a callback, stored in a field, or taken with &.
     They ARE used, but every call goes through a pointer, so every
     fan-in-based number understates them.
ACT read these as live API surface; a pointer-dispatched function is a
     plugin point or a registered handler.
MISLEADS only uses inside function BODIES are here. A name listed in a
     file-scope initializer (the dominant dispatch-table pattern) is in
     dispatch-table-orphan instead. `addr_taken` also counts `&x` of a
     local that happens to share the function's name.
Declared in a prototype, never defined in the tree

ANSWERS names with a prototype/extern declaration but no definition
     anywhere in the tree: either the definition lives in a library
     this run skipped (fine), or the symbol is promised but missing
     (a link error waiting for the first caller).
ACT for each row decide: library boundary (ignore) or genuinely
     missing (define or delete the prototype).
MISLEADS a definition behind `#ifdef` that the scan excluded reads as
     missing; static functions are excluded from the definition side
     only when their name matches -- a same-named static in one file
     does NOT satisfy an extern promise in another; libc prototypes in
     system headers are not scanned (only this tree's files are).
access(X) then open(X) on the same variable (CERT POS01-C)

ANSWERS functions that both access(X) and open(X) with the same
     variable: the permission check and the use are two system calls,
     and the file can be swapped between them. The window is the whole
     race.
ACT open first, then fstat the descriptor; never trust access for
     security decisions.
MISLEADS same-function variable-name pairing, not data flow: access on
     a path built from a different variable than the open is missed,
     and access+open on a CONSTANT path (no race on most filesystems
     in practice) reads the same as the race; `faccessat` with
     AT_EACCESS is a different capture and is absent.
Acquires a lock more often than it releases it

ANSWERS the functions where an early return or a goto-out ladder can
     leave a mutex held: acquire sites outnumber release sites in one
     body. The next caller to take that lock blocks forever -- and if
     the lock is taken under load first, the hang looks like a load
     problem, not a code problem.
ACT pair every acquire with a release on EVERY path, or move to
     pthread_mutex_trylock with explicit unlock on the failure path.
MISLEADS counts SITES, not paths: two acquires and two releases can
     still leak (both releases behind the same `if`), and a function
     whose contract is 'returns with the lock held' (an allocator's
     arena lock, a lazy initializer) is correct and lands here anyway.
     A release inside a called cleanup function is invisible. A call is
     a lock operation when one WORD of its name is lock, unlock, trylock,
     rdlock, wrlock, mutex or the like (pthread_mutex_lock, spin_unlock,
     LOCK): a project wrapper named otherwise is not seen at all.
A lock is held across a call that can sleep or block I/O

ANSWERS where a function both takes a lock and performs raw descriptor
     I/O in the same body: read/write/recv/send/mmap while holding a
     pthread mutex. Every other thread wanting that lock stalls for the
     duration of the I/O -- the classic latency cliff under load, and
     with a non-recursive mutex plus a nested acquisition, a deadlock.
ACT shrink the critical section: copy what is needed under the lock,
     release, then do the I/O. If the I/O must be covered, document why
     and bound it (timeout, O_NONBLOCK).
MISLEADS co-occurrence in one body is not ordering: the I/O may run
     strictly before the first acquire or after the last release, and
     this cannot see which. Buffered stdio (fprintf) is excluded here
     on purpose -- it lives in its own query family; a blocking call
     reached THROUGH a callee while the lock is held is invisible.
Copy whose size argument names neither dst nor src

ANSWERS the copy sites where the SIZE expression dereferences a
     buffer that is neither argument: memcpy(a, b, sizeof(c)) copies
     by c's width -- CERT ARR38-C's shape when a, b and c have
     different element sizes. `size_buf` is the identifier the size
     expression references (from its sizeof), '' when it names none.
ACT read every row: the fix is a size naming THE DESTINATION, or an
     explicit MIN of both. Prefer strlcpy / memcpy_s where available.
MISLEADS textual, not semantic: sizeof(*dst) vs sizeof(struct x) can
     be equal; copying into a larger dst is legal; a length VARIABLE
     as size reads clean here but is exactly where an unchecked value
     bites -- this query finds the WRONG-BUFFER sites, not every bad
     copy. Argument capture stops at one paren level.
malloc(n * k) with no sizeof in the size expression

ANSWERS allocation sites whose size expression names no sizeof at all:
     malloc(count * 4) hard-codes the element width, malloc(len) may be
     confusing bytes with elements, and neither survives the element
     type changing under it. Each row is the exact line to re-derive.
ACT write sizeof(*p) (or sizeof(T)) explicitly, and prefer calloc for
     arrays so the overflow check is someone else's already-written bug
     fix.
MISLEADS a byte-oriented API (a raw network buffer, a string + 1) is
     CORRECT without sizeof and will dominate this list in most trees;
     a size expression built through a project macro (`s_malloc`,
     `ALLOC_ARRAY`) hides its sizeof from this scan entirely.
Functions that WRITE file-scope state, ranked by how much they touch

ANSWERS which functions mutate shared file-scope objects, and which
     globals are written from the most places. `race-surface` says a
     global EXISTS and is mutable; this says WHO actually writes it --
     the half that turns 'could race' into 'here is the commit that
     must take the lock'.
ACT every writer of a hot global is a serialization point: batch the
     writes, shard the state, or make the field atomic.
MISLEADS same-file globals only -- writes through an extern declared
     in a header are invisible, so cross-TU writers undercount; a
     local variable shadowing a global name is counted as the global;
     and `g->field = x` through a pointer parameter reads as a write
     only when the base name matches a captured global.
Fixed-width narrowing casts on data that came from wide sources

ANSWERS `(uint32_t)x`-style casts to a STRICTLY narrower fixed-width
     type in functions that also do heavy arithmetic or I/O -- the
     places where a 64-bit length, hash or offset silently becomes 32
     bits. The wrap is not UB, which is exactly why nothing complains:
     the value just comes back wrong on input above 4 GiB.
ACT before casting, range-check and reject; after casting, never use
     the wide original again. Prefer size_t end-to-end.
MISLEADS a cast to uint8_t for serialization into a wire format is
     correct and common; the scan cannot know the value fits. Only
     fixed-width targets are counted -- casts to int/long are
     platform-dependent and deliberately absent.
Signed value compared against a size or sizeof result

ANSWERS comparisons like `i < sizeof(b)` or `n <= len` where one side is a
     local or parameter DECLARED signed (int, long, ssize_t ...) and the
     other is a sizeof, a strlen, or a name declared size_t/unsigned. The
     signed side converts, so -1 becomes SIZE_MAX and the bounds check
     PASSES for the one input that must fail it (CERT INT31-C).
ACT make the index size_t, or compare in the signed domain against a
     checked cast of the size.
MISLEADS types come from declarations in the same function only: a struct
     member, a global or a call other than strlen has no known type and is
     never the size side, so this list is a floor. A value proven
     non-negative before the compare makes its row harmless.
Variadic function forwarding to a vprintf-family call

ANSWERS the wrappers that turn caller-supplied arguments into formatted
     output: variadic definitions containing v?snprintf/v?printf/syslog.
     Whether %n is reachable from outside depends ENTIRELY on whether
     these forwarders pass through a caller-controlled format string --
     they are the chokepoints worth auditing, because every other
     printf-shaped call in the tree funnels through a handful of them.
ACT audit each: the format argument should be a literal or a fixed
     table entry, never a parameter forwarded verbatim.
MISLEADS a wrapper that hardcodes its own literal format ('%s') is safe
     and indistinguishable here from one forwarding the caller's format
     through; the format STRING itself is blanked during scanning (it is
     a literal), so its content is not inspected.
Referenced ONLY in file-scope initializers: live but zero fan-in

ANSWERS functions kept alive exclusively by a dispatch-table entry at
     file scope -- an initializer reference (`static cmd_t cmds[] =
     {&get, &set}`) or a generated-table argument
     (`MAKE_CMD(...,getCommand,...)`). No body contains the use, so
     dead-code and every fan-in-based number read zero while the
     function is very much alive: these are the plugin points of a
     table-driven C program.
ACT treat as public API: renaming one breaks a TABLE, silently, at
     runtime. Any signature change needs the table's owning module in
     the review. `refs` says how many tables list it.
MISLEADS the capture is textual (argument position, file scope, macro
     bodies skipped), so a same-named DATA object referenced in an
     initializer can attach to a function of that name after pruning;
     a table entry spelled through a project macro's PARAMETER is not
     seen (macro bodies are excluded on purpose); and a function whose
     address is taken BOTH in a table and in a body appears here only
     for its body-level rows.
Allocations whose frees sit only behind error branches

ANSWERS functions that allocate, free, and branch heavily: the shape
    where the free list covers the error ladder but a NEW success-path
    early return skips it. Unlike ownership-review (which flags 'no
    free at all'), this finds the functions where a future edit is most
    likely to introduce a leak, because the discipline exists but is
    one return away from breaking. `allocs` counts direct
    malloc/calloc/realloc/alloca sites; project wrappers are invisible
    to it.
ACT when editing one of these, trace every new return against the free
    ladder -- or convert to goto-cleanup, which makes skipping it
    impossible.
MISLEADS a heuristic by construction: alloc==free==1 with two branches
    is usually fine; the ranking surfaces DENSITY of exits vs frees,
    not an actual missing free. Transfers of ownership (returning the
    buffer) look identical, and frees reached through a wrapper
    function do not count, so a disciplined function using one can
    read as frees=0 -- those land in ownership-review instead.
p = realloc(p, n): the old block is lost on failure

ANSWERS where a failed realloc leaks the buffer it was resizing.
ACT assign to a TEMPORARY: `tmp = realloc(p, n); if (!tmp) { /* p is still
     valid */ } else p = tmp;`.
MISLEADS matched textually on `x = realloc(x,`, so a realloc through a wrapper,
     or one whose result lands in a different variable, is missed. A realloc to
     a SMALLER size does not fail in practice, so some rows are noise.
An allocation sized from strlen() with no room for the terminator

ANSWERS where the size expression is a string length and nothing adds one.
ACT MEM35-C: `strlen(s) + 1`, or use strdup, which cannot get this wrong.
MISLEADS only sites whose size text contains `strlen` AND no `+` at all are
     listed, so `strlen(s) + sizeof(hdr)` is excluded -- correctly, since that
     may be a counted buffer. The size is TEXT, not a value: a length computed
     two statements earlier is invisible here.
Descriptors and FILEs opened on more paths than they are closed

ANSWERS where an open outnumbers its close inside one function.
ACT FIO42-C: every open needs a close on EVERY path, including the error
     returns and the goto-out ladder. Prefer one cleanup label.
MISLEADS a function that opens and hands the descriptor to its caller is
     correct and looks identical. Opens and closes reached through a wrapper
     are not counted, and a resource closed by the caller reads as a leak.
Allocates and never compares anything to NULL

ANSWERS functions where no allocation result is checked at all.
ACT ERR33-C: on a 25k-function tree this list is long and mostly test code and
     wrappers -- narrow it with --module and read the high fan_in rows first.
MISLEADS `n_null_check` counts `== NULL` and `if (!x)` only. A check inside a
     macro (`serverAssert(x)`), a helper, or an `assert(x)` is not seen, and a
     wrapper that checks centrally makes every one of its callers look guilty.
A variable-length array whose extent someone else chose

ANSWERS stack allocations sized by a non-constant, worst where the length
     arrives from I/O or from a string operation.
ACT ARR32-C: bound the length before the declaration, or heap-allocate. A VLA
     has no failure mode -- it simply writes past the frame.
MISLEADS the filter is `n_io>0 OR n_memory>0 OR recursive`, a PROXY for
     "the length may be attacker-influenced", not evidence of it. A VLA sized
     from a local constant is still listed if the function also does I/O.
A name is freed and then dereferenced later in the same body

ANSWERS the MEM30-C use-after-free shape that one function can contain.
ACT every row needs a read of the code: the dereference may sit on a path where
     the pointer was reassigned, which is correct.
MISLEADS textual and scope-limited. It cannot see that the two are on mutually
     exclusive branches, or that the pointer was reassigned between them.
     `p = malloc(...)` after a free is excluded; `*p = ...` is counted. A free
     at the bottom of a loop that reallocates at the top is the common false
     positive -- and the loop column is the only hint offered.
rand() and friends where unpredictability might matter

ANSWERS MSC30-C: the places a predictable generator is used.
ACT anything key-, token-, nonce-, or salt-related here is a finding.
     Everything else -- shuffling test data, jitter, backoff -- is fine and is
     still listed.
MISLEADS presence, not reachability. Nothing here says the value is observable
     by an attacker; the `io` and `exec` columns are the only evidence offered.
Shifts by an identifier rather than a literal

ANSWERS INT34-C: shift counts the reader cannot check at the shift site.
ACT a count that can be negative, or >= the width of the promoted left operand,
     is undefined. Clamp at the source, not at every shift.
MISLEADS the great majority of these are correct bit-twiddling with a constant
     named for readability. This ranks where to LOOK, and the count is of SITES,
     not of bugs.
Where the errno error channel is load bearing

ANSWERS the functions whose error reporting depends on a global that any
     intervening call can overwrite.
ACT ERR30-C: for each row, check that nothing runs between the failing call and
     the errno read. Ranked by read count, because that is where a clobber hurts.
MISLEADS it cannot tell a correct read from a stale one -- only that the code
     consults errno at all. A function that reads errno correctly on every path
     and one that reads it after three intervening printf calls look identical.
getenv(): the process environment as an input

ANSWERS every place the environment is read.
ACT the environment is attacker-controlled wherever the process was started by
     a less trusted one. A length from getenv needs the same bounds treatment
     as a length from a socket.
MISLEADS presence only. A path from getenv used with an explicit length is fine;
     one concatenated into a command or a path is not. The `exec` and `mem`
     columns are the triage hint, not a verdict.
An assert() that does work, which NDEBUG deletes

ANSWERS assertions whose removal would change behaviour.
ACT move the work out of the assert and assert on its RESULT. Under NDEBUG the
     assert vanishes and so does whatever it did.
MISLEADS the match is a shape (`=`, `++`, memcpy, malloc, printf inside the
     parens), so `assert(x == y)` is excluded correctly but `assert(f(&x))` with
     a read-only f is still counted. Test files are excluded; test helpers that
     live in source files are not.
Two locks taken in both orders by different functions

ANSWERS the CON35-C / POS51-C deadlock shape.
ACT for each row decide whether the two functions can run at the same time.
     If yes, this is a deadlock waiting on scheduling; if no, it is an invariant
     someone should write down next to the lock.
MISLEADS order is inferred from LINE NUMBER inside a function, not from control
     flow: two acquires on one line, or one inside a conditional that actually
     runs first, are ordered by text. Only lock-SHAPED identifiers are recorded,
     so a lock held in a variable (`myLockAcquire(lock, ...)`) is invisible and
     every ordering involving it is missed entirely.
Two or more fields sharing one 64-byte cache line

ANSWERS where independent writes to one struct will invalidate each other.
ACT only matters if different threads write different fields of one instance.
     Aligning the hot field is the cheap fix; splitting the struct is the real
     one.
MISLEADS nothing here knows which fields are written by which thread. The
     `conc_fns_in_module` column is the only evidence offered: how many
     functions in the same module touch a concurrency primitive at all. Offsets
     are LP64 and reported only where the layout was computed exactly.
strncpy/strncat sized with sizeof: no terminator guaranteed

ANSWERS the STR31-C / STR32-C shape: a copy that fills the buffer exactly and
     adds no NUL when the source is that long or longer.
ACT `strncpy(d, s, sizeof d - 1); d[sizeof d - 1] = '\0';`, or use a function
     that always terminates.
MISLEADS matched on the SIZE ARGUMENT TEXT, so `strncpy(d, s, n)` with a runtime
     n -- which can overrun for a different reason -- is absent. A size that is
     provably shorter than the buffer is listed anyway.
Structs with alignment holes that are copied or written whole

ANSWERS DCL39-C: where padding bytes can be stored or transmitted.
ACT if the struct crosses a trust boundary -- to disk, to the wire, to another
     process -- serialise it field by field, or pack and re-order it so there
     are no holes.
MISLEADS `copied_whole` counts memcpy-family sites in the same FILE as the
     struct, not copies OF that struct: it is a proxy, not a data-flow fact.
     Padding is computed only where every field's type could be sized, so a
     struct containing an unknown typedef is absent rather than wrong. There
     is no fan_in column: nothing calls a struct, so it would read 0 on
     every row of every corpus -- the ranking is by pad bytes and copy
     sites instead.
static functions nothing calls and whose address is never taken

ANSWERS unreachable code, with the stronger claim `static` allows.
ACT `static` means no other translation unit can reach it, so unlike dead-code
     this is a candidate for deletion rather than for investigation.
MISLEADS a static function reached through a function pointer assigned in a
     macro or a generated table escapes the addr_taken test and appears here
     while alive. Grep the name as a string before deleting anything.
External functions defined in a .c with no prototype anywhere

ANSWERS MISRA-C 8.2 / CERT DCL40-C: where callers get no signature check.
ACT add the prototype to the header that owns this module. Without one, every
     caller in another translation unit is calling an implicitly-declared
     function and an argument mismatch is silent.
MISLEADS a prototype in a header this run did not parse -- vendored, generated,
     or excluded -- is invisible, so those rows are wrong. It also does not
     check that a prototype which DOES exist agrees with the definition.

ANSWERS headers that cannot safely be included twice.
ACT one line: `#ifndef FOO_H` / `#define FOO_H` ... `#endif`, or `#pragma once`.
MISLEADS a guard is detected as an `#ifndef` in the first 12 lines, so a header
     that uses ONLY `#pragma once` is reported as unguarded, which is wrong --
     the preprocessor table does not record pragmas. Ranked by how many files
     include it, since an unguarded header nobody includes twice harms nobody.
Module pairs that can each reach the other through calls

ANSWERS the dependency cycles: seams that cannot be cut.
ACT a cycle means neither side can be built, tested, or reasoned about alone.
     Break it by inverting one edge -- a callback, an interface header, an event.
MISLEADS depth-bounded at 4 hops in each direction, so a longer return path
     reads as no cycle. Modules are two path components, so a cycle WITHIN one
     module is invisible here by construction.
Functions that break their own file's dominant name prefix

ANSWERS C's missing namespace, made visible.
ACT either the function is misplaced and belongs in the file that owns its
     prefix, or the file is doing two jobs and should be split.
MISLEADS the dominant prefix is simply the most common one in the file, so a
     file with no dominant convention is skipped entirely (fewer than three
     users) and a file with two legitimate conventions reports half of itself.
     The prefix is the text before the first underscore.
Widely-called functions with no caller in any test file

ANSWERS where a regression would ship.
ACT these are the highest-value test targets: high fan_in means a bug here
     reaches far, and no test currently reaches it at all.
MISLEADS "reached by a test" means a resolved call edge from a file this run
     classified as a test. A test that drives the code through a socket, a
     subprocess, or a function pointer produces no edge and reads as untested.
A syscall inside a loop body: one per iteration

ANSWERS where the syscall count scales with the data.
ACT batch it: readv/writev, a larger buffer, or hoist the call out of the loop.
MISLEADS a loop over a handful of descriptors is correct and is listed. The
     count is of call SITES in loop bodies, so one site in a hot loop beats ten
     in a cold one -- which the ranking cannot see. `io_in_loop` has been
     captured and indexed since the base schema and no query read it until now.
A lock acquired inside a loop body

ANSWERS where a lock is taken once per iteration instead of once per pass.
ACT hoist it, or take it around the batch. The cost is not the lock, it is the
     queue behind it.
MISLEADS a lock released at the end of each iteration may be REQUIRED -- a
     per-item invariant, or a condvar wait. Loop depth is the triage hint:
     depth 1 over a short loop is rarely the problem.
Branches inside loop bodies, ranked by how many

ANSWERS where the predictor re-decides on every iteration.
ACT only worth acting on where the branch is data-dependent. The switch and
     call columns are the ones that usually are.
MISLEADS this is the single most common shape in real code -- every loop has at
     least one branch, including its own condition. It is a ranking of VOLUME,
     not a finding, and a perfectly predicted branch costs almost nothing.
Edge-triggered registration with no EAGAIN drain anywhere in the function

ANSWERS the stall. epoll(7): with EPOLLET the caller "must consider it ready
     until the next (nonblocking) read/write yields EAGAIN". Reading once and
     moving on leaves the rest of the buffer in the kernel, and the next
     epoll_wait() blocks forever -- the peer is waiting on a reply to bytes
     this process has already been told about. EV_CLEAR is kqueue's spelling
     of the same contract.
ACT loop until EAGAIN, or drop EPOLLET/EV_CLEAR and take level-triggered.
MISLEADS the drain usually lives in a DIFFERENT function from the
     registration -- a helper reads until EAGAIN and this ranks the registrar,
     because that is the only place the flag is visible. Both counts are
     per function and a project that centralises the drain will list every
     registration site. It also cannot see that the descriptor is a datagram,
     where one read really can consume everything.
A blocking wait whose return value is used without any EINTR handling

ANSWERS where a delivered signal becomes a spin or a silent stall.
ACT epoll_wait(2), kevent(2) and io_uring_wait_cqe(3) all return -1 with
     errno EINTR on any signal. Test for it and retry; do not fall through
     into the loop with a negative count.
MISLEADS the test is the presence of the token EINTR in the function -- a
     retry in a shared wrapper does not make the caller clean, and a
     `continue` on EINTR in a loop this function does not contain is
     invisible. Conversely a function that names EINTR for an unrelated
     syscall reads clean.
Write-readiness registered and never withdrawn: a level-triggered busy loop

ANSWERS the 100%-CPU-forever shape.
ACT EPOLLOUT and EVFILT_WRITE are level-triggered, so they are ready whenever
     the socket can take a single byte -- which is nearly always. Register
     them only when there is something queued, and remove them with
     EPOLL_CTL_DEL / EV_DELETE the moment the queue drains.
MISLEADS the deregistration may be in another function, and a project that
     manages its write interest centrally will show every ADD site here.
     EV_DELETE is also the normal teardown path, so a function that registers
     and then tears down the whole connection counts as clean only if the
     two are in the same body.
A poller that never looks at the error or hangup flags

ANSWERS where disconnects and registration failures are silently dropped.
ACT epoll(7) delivers EPOLLERR and EPOLLHUP whether or not they were
     requested, and kqueue(2) sets EV_EOF and EV_ERROR the same way. Test
     them before the read/write flags, or a closed peer is reported as a
     readable descriptor forever.
MISLEADS the flags may be handled by a shared dispatcher rather than here,
     which is the common and correct design; this ranks the functions that
     own the mask, not the ones that get it right. A loop that only ever
     watches timers or signals has no error flag to handle and still appears.
Delivered-once registration with no re-arm: the descriptor goes silent

ANSWERS where a file descriptor stops reporting events permanently.
ACT EPOLLONESHOT disables the descriptor after one delivery and it stays
     disabled until epoll_ctl(2) with EPOLL_CTL_MOD re-arms it -- ADD does
     not re-arm, it only registers. EV_DISPATCH on kqueue needs EV_ENABLE.
     Either re-arm or drop the flag.
MISLEADS EPOLL_CTL_ADD is deliberately NOT counted as a re-arm, so a
     register/delete/re-add cycle reads as unre-armed even though it works.
     The re-arm is also usually in the I/O handler, not the registering
     function.
CQEs consumed without ever testing res: io_uring errors are invisible

ANSWERS where every I/O error becomes a successful zero-length operation.
ACT io_uring(7) is explicit: "errno is never used for passing back error
     information. Instead, res will contain ... -errno." Test `cqe->res < 0`
     on every completion, including the ones from a batched submit.
MISLEADS the test is a textual match for `res` in the function, so a helper
     that checks it centrally leaves every caller listed. Multi-shot and
     IORING_CQE_F_MORE completions need the check on each one, which this
     cannot distinguish from a single check.
io_uring used together with errno: the wrong error channel

ANSWERS a porting bug, and the most common one when synchronous I/O is
     converted to io_uring.
ACT res carries the error. Reading errno after an io_uring operation reports
     whatever the last unrelated call left behind -- and under SQPOLL there
     may have been no syscall at all to set it.
MISLEADS errno may be read here for a genuinely synchronous call in the same
     function -- an open(), an mmap(), a malloc() failure. The columns show
     both counts side by side precisely so that judgement is possible;
     nothing here proves the errno belongs to the io_uring call.
SQPOLL ring with a free in the same function: freed before completion

ANSWERS a use-after-free that the kernel dereferences, not this process.
ACT io_uring(7): without SQPOLL a submitted pointer only has to stay valid
     until io_uring_submit() returns; WITH IORING_SETUP_SQPOLL it "must
     remain valid until completion". Hold the buffer until its CQE arrives,
     or drop SQPOLL.
MISLEADS the free may be of something entirely unrelated to the submission,
     and a function that both submits and frees a scratch buffer is listed
     regardless of whether the two are connected. The flag is captured from
     the body, so a ring configured in another function and passed in is
     invisible here. There is no fan_in column: SQPOLL setup with a free
     in the same body is nearly always a test's main(), which has no
     callers, so the number measured 0 on every row of every corpus.
Shared ring head or tail touched with no acquire/release barrier

ANSWERS a data race on memory the kernel is writing at the same time.
ACT the head and tail are shared with the kernel and both sides write them,
     so io_uring(7) requires an acquire on the way in and a release on the
     way out. Use the io_uring_smp_load_acquire / io_uring_smp_store_release
     helpers or their C11 equivalents; a plain read is not sufficient.
MISLEADS the ring reference is matched by NAME SHAPE -- an identifier
     containing `ring` followed within a short distance by `head` or `tail`
     -- so a project's own ring that does not use the word, or a raw
     integer index into the ring, is missed. liburing wraps all of this and
     a ring accessed only through it is correctly absent.
Allocation on the event path: one malloc per event

ANSWERS where the allocator is on the hot path of the whole process.
ACT per-event allocations dominate a saturated loop. Use a pool, a slab, or
     an object cache keyed by the descriptor; the allocation should not scale
     with the event rate.
MISLEADS the allocation may be a one-time setup that merely shares a body
     with the wait, and the count is of SITES, not of events. A loop that
     allocates only on connection establishment -- not per event -- looks
     identical here.
A wait primitive called with an indefinite or zero timeout

ANSWERS which loops can never do periodic work, and which never sleep.
ACT two opposite bugs, both from the same argument. NULL or -1 blocks until
     an event arrives, so the loop can never run a timer, check a shutdown
     flag, or re-arm -- the usual fix is a bounded timeout plus a periodic
     tick. 0 turns the wait into a poll, and a loop polling at 0 burns a
     core to save microseconds of latency it usually does not need.
MISLEADS an indefinite wait is CORRECT wherever the loop has nothing to do
     between events -- postgres's WaitEventSetWaitBlock blocks forever
     precisely because no timeout was requested. This ranks the property,
     not the defect; read the fan_in column before acting. Only epoll_wait
     and kevent are analysed: io_uring's wait calls end in an out-parameter
     or a count, so "the last argument is the timeout" is not true there.
