     skipped -- counting it was 2 of redis's first 3 rows. There is no
     fan_in column: an event-loop poll function is almost always reached
     through a dispatch-table pointer, so it has no callers and the number
     measured 0 on every row of every corpus.
Edge-triggered registration on a descriptor never made non-blocking

ANSWERS the other half of the edge-triggered contract.
ACT epoll(7): an EPOLLET application "should use nonblocking file
     descriptors to avoid having a blocking read or write starve a task that
     is handling multiple file descriptors". Set O_NONBLOCK (or accept with
     SOCK_NONBLOCK) before registering.
MISLEADS the flag is usually set somewhere ELSE -- at accept time, in the
     listen socket, or by a shared helper -- so a correct loop is listed
     whenever the descriptor was made non-blocking in a different function.
     EAGAIN handling and a non-blocking descriptor are two separate halves:
     et-without-drain ranks the first, this ranks the second, and a loop can
     fail either one.
Creates a poller instance and never releases anything in the function

ANSWERS where an epoll descriptor, a kqueue, or a ring is dropped.
ACT these are descriptors (and for io_uring, two shared mappings). close()
     the epoll fd and the kqueue, and call io_uring_queue_exit() with any
     registered buffers or files unregistered first -- on every error path,
     not only the happy one.
MISLEADS the release test is any close()/queue_exit()/unregister() call in
     the same function, so a function that closes an unrelated descriptor
     reads clean, and a constructor that hands the instance to its caller
     -- which is the correct design -- is listed as a leak. Ownership
     transfer is invisible here.
io_uring_get_sqe() whose result is never checked for NULL

ANSWERS the most common io_uring bug there is.
ACT io_uring_get_sqe() returns NULL when the submission queue is full. Keep
     the queue drained, size it for the intended depth, and test the pointer
     before filling it in -- otherwise a busy ring is a NULL dereference.
MISLEADS the test is the function-wide count of `== NULL` and `if (!x)`, so
     an unrelated NULL check anywhere in the function makes it read clean,
     and a check inside a shared helper does not. Ranked by how many SQEs
     the function takes, because that is how often it can be NULL.
Completions waited for but never returned to the kernel

ANSWERS where the completion ring can fill and stall the program silently.
ACT every CQE has to be marked seen -- io_uring_cqe_seen(), or
     io_uring_cq_advance() for a batch. Until it is, the slot stays occupied;
     when the ring is full the kernel cannot post another completion and the
     ring stops making progress with no error anywhere.
MISLEADS a function that peeks rather than waits, or one that hands the CQE
     to a helper that advances it, is listed. liburing's *_nr and
     for_each_cqe helpers all advance in the caller, so this is usually a
     true positive; the gap is a project's own wrapper.
More SQEs taken than user_data values set: completions cannot be correlated

ANSWERS where a completion cannot be matched to the request it belongs to.
ACT io_uring(7) is explicit that completions arrive in ANY order and that
     "the most common method" of matching them is the user_data field. Set
     it on every SQE that shares a ring with another in-flight request, or
     use liburing's io_uring_sqe_set_data().
MISLEADS this only matters when more than one request is in flight at a
     time, so the query requires at least 2 SQEs; a submit-one-wait-one loop
     legitimately needs none. The comparison is of COUNTS, not of identity:
     a function that sets user_data on one SQE and not on the other reads as
     half-clean. liburing tests that reuse a single request are listed too.
Stream sends or receives with no IOSQE_IO_LINK anywhere

ANSWERS where two stream operations on one socket can be reordered.
ACT io_uring(7): "it is generally unsafe to have more than one outstanding
     send, or more than one outstanding receive ... on a given socket at a
     time, as the kernel may reorder their execution." Link them with
     IOSQE_IO_LINK, submit them in one batch, or wait between them.
MISLEADS two sends of INDEPENDENT data -- a header and a separate response,
     on different sockets -- are fine unlinked, and this cannot tell them
     apart: it sees prep_send twice and no link flag. Datagram sockets are
     unaffected by the ordering rule and are still listed.
A ring initialised in this function with no io_uring_queue_exit

ANSWERS where a ring's descriptor and its two shared mappings are dropped.
ACT io_uring_queue_exit() releases the ring, the mappings and the
     descriptor. Registered buffers and files must be unregistered first.
     Put it on every exit path.
MISLEADS a function that builds a ring and hands it to its caller is
     correct and is listed -- ownership transfer is invisible to a
     per-function count. Short-lived test and example code frequently lets
     process exit do the cleanup, which is why this ranks high on trees
     that are mostly tests.
EVFILT_TIMER registered with a data value of zero

ANSWERS a timer that does not mean what it says.
ACT kqueue(2): "Periodic timers with a specified timeout of 0 will be
     silently adjusted to timeout after 1 of the time units specified by
     the requested precision in fflags." At NOTE_NSECONDS that is a
     one-nanosecond periodic timer -- the loop never sleeps and the process
     pins a core. Pass the interval you meant, or use EV_ONESHOT.
MISLEADS only EV_SET's data argument is inspected, so a timer whose value
     is assigned afterwards (`kev.data = 0`) is missed, and a data of 0 that
     is genuinely intended as "one unit" reads as a bug. NOTE_ABSTIME
     timers are exempt in spirit but not in this test.
EV_RECEIPT bulk registration whose EV_ERROR events are never read

ANSWERS where a failed registration is silent.
ACT kqueue(2): with EV_RECEIPT, "EV_ERROR [is] always returned. When a
     filter is successfully added the data field will be zero." The failures
     arrive as EVENTS, not as a return value -- so iterate the eventlist and
     test EV_ERROR on each, or drop EV_RECEIPT and check kevent()'s return.
MISLEADS the EV_ERROR test may live in a shared dispatcher. This is the
     rarest of the kqueue shapes and neither test corpus uses EV_RECEIPT at
     all, so its only evidence is the fixture.
A loop that waits, and also blocks on something else inside the loop

ANSWERS where one slow descriptor stalls all the others.
ACT an event loop must block on exactly one thing: the wait primitive. A
     synchronous read inside the body stalls every other descriptor for its
     duration, and a lock taken in the body serialises every thread that
     wants the same lock. Move the work off the loop, or make it
     non-blocking and continue on the next event.
MISLEADS the per-loop counters cover EVERY loop in the function, not only
     the event loop, so a helper called from the loop that happens to lock
     makes the whole function look blocking. Locking to update a shared
     statistic is usually correct and cheap; the ranking cannot tell a
     contended lock from an uncontended one.
snprintf's return is never compared to anything

ANSWERS where truncated output is silently accepted.
ACT snprintf returns the length it WOULD have written. Compare it against
     the buffer size and treat `>= sizeof buf` as truncation. Otherwise
     "fit exactly" and "lost 400 bytes" are the same result.
MISLEADS the guard test is function-wide (`< 0`, `== -1`, `>= size`), so a
     check for an unrelated call makes a row read clean. This is the single
     largest rule in the pack by measured volume: 296 rows across the four
     corpora, so triage by fan_in rather than reading top to bottom. GCC's
     `-Wformat-truncation` catches some of these at compile time, but only
     when the buffer size is known there.

ANSWERS where a short read, a failed write, or an unconverted field passes.
ACT fread returns a COUNT, not a success flag -- compare it to the count you
     asked for. fscanf returns the number of conversions; check it equals the
     number of specifiers, or the untouched variables hold garbage.
MISLEADS function-wide guard test. A loop that checks nothing but writes
     into a buffer it then validates another way is a false positive; there
     is no way to see that from here.
strtol-family result used without errno and end pointer

ANSWERS where "0", "not a number" and "overflow" are indistinguishable.
ACT strtol fails three ways. Set `errno = 0` first, pass a real end pointer,
     then check endptr != input AND errno != ERANGE. One without the other
     is not a check.
MISLEADS requires BOTH guards, so a function that clears errno but ignores
     the end pointer is listed. `atoi` is worse still and is a separate
     smell this query does not cover.
isalpha/toupper called on a plain char

ANSWERS a latent undefined behaviour that is invisible until a byte >= 0x80.
ACT ctype functions are defined only for values representable as an unsigned
     char, or EOF. Pass `(unsigned char)c`, or hold the byte in an `int`.
     With a negative `char` the result is undefined -- typically a read
     outside the table.
MISLEADS the guard is `(unsigned char)` anywhere in the function, so a cast
     used for an unrelated conversion makes a row read clean; and a char
     that provably never goes negative (ASCII literals) is still listed.
     ctype had ZERO coverage before this rule.

ANSWERS where a signal shortens a sleep and nobody notices.
ACT on -1/EINTR the remainder is undone. Retry with the remainder
     (nanosleep writes it into the second argument) or the sleep is short.
MISLEADS the test is the token EINTR anywhere in the function. Some sleeps
     genuinely should be interruptible -- an alarm-driven timeout loop is
     correct and is listed.
send/write return never compared: a short write truncates

ANSWERS where a message can be silently truncated at the receiver.
ACT send/write return the number of bytes accepted, which is often less than
     the length. Loop until everything is sent, or treat a short count as an
     error, depending on the protocol.
MISLEADS fires on any send/write in an unguarded function, including writes
     to a blocking file where a short write genuinely cannot happen. It
     cannot tell a socket from a file descriptor -- the two share write().
mmap with no munmap anywhere in the function

ANSWERS where address space is acquired and never released.
ACT pair every mmap with munmap on every path. On a long-running daemon this
     is a slow exhaustion rather than a crash.
MISLEADS ownership transfer is invisible: a helper that returns the mapping
     to its caller is correct and is listed. Short-lived processes that let
     exit() clean up are listed too -- which is why liburing's tests rank
     high here.

ANSWERS where a signal death is reported as an exit code.
ACT the status word must be decoded first. WIFEXITED gates WEXITSTATUS;
     WIFSIGNALED gates WTERMSIG. Reading it raw conflates the two.
MISLEADS function-wide guard test; the macros may appear in a helper.

ANSWERS where malformed input silently yields uninitialised variables.
ACT scanf returns the number of successful conversions. Check it equals the
     number of specifiers. Prefer fgets + strtol, which is checkable.
MISLEADS function-wide guard test.

ANSWERS where a NaN is born and then propagates silently.
ACT sqrt of a negative, log of zero, asin outside [-1,1] are domain errors:
     they return NaN and set errno. Clamp the argument or check the result
     with isnan().
MISLEADS the guard is any comparison or `if` in the function, which is a weak
     proxy -- it cannot tell a clamp on THIS argument from an unrelated
     branch. Only 7 rows across the corpora; gcc's -Wfloat-equal and clang's
     -Wtautological-compare-ish checks do not cover this.

ANSWERS where two threads can read each other's formatted time.
ACT these return a pointer to a single static object. Use the _r variants
     (localtime_r, gmtime_r) or ctime_r, which fill a caller buffer.
MISLEADS single-threaded programs are entirely unaffected and are listed.
     The `conc_in_fn` column is the only evidence offered: whether the same
     function touches a concurrency primitive at all.

ANSWERS where handler semantics depend on the platform.
ACT signal() has implementation-defined behaviour on delivery -- SysV resets
     the handler, BSD does not. sigaction() makes it explicit and is
     portable.
MISLEADS signal() is not wrong everywhere, only where the reset semantics
     matter. A program that reinstalls its own handler is fine and listed.
mmap compared to NULL instead of MAP_FAILED

ANSWERS a check that passes on failure.
ACT mmap fails with MAP_FAILED, which is (void *)-1 on most systems and NOT
     NULL. A NULL check succeeds, and the caller then dereferences -1.
MISLEADS the guard test looks for MAP_FAILED or a NULL check; a codebase
     that correctly checks MAP_FAILED only via a macro is missed. Only 2
     rows across the corpora -- rare, and worth finding precisely because
     it is rare.

ANSWERS where one slow peer can stall the loop that accepted it.
ACT an accepted socket starts blocking. Set O_NONBLOCK (or accept with
     SOCK_NONBLOCK) before handing it to an event loop, or a read can block
     every other descriptor.
MISLEADS the guard is O_NONBLOCK/SOCK_NONBLOCK/F_SETFL anywhere in the
     function, so a non-blocking set performed in a helper is missed and the
     accepting function is listed.
va_start with no va_end in the same function

ANSWERS where a va_list is left in an undefined state.
ACT every va_start needs a matching va_end on every path -- including the
     early returns. On some ABIs the frame is not cleaned up without it.
MISLEADS only 2 rows across the corpora; this is a rare bug, kept because it
     is cheap and unambiguous. A va_end reached through a macro is missed.
Array sized with SIGSTKSZ / MINSIGSTKSZ / PTHREAD_STACK_MIN

ANSWERS a mis-sized buffer that appeared when glibc changed underneath it.
ACT glibc 2.34 made these non-constant -- they are sysconf() calls now.
     Query them at runtime (sysconf(_SC_SIGSTKSZ)) and allocate, or use a
     constant of your own. A compile-time array gets a size that is no
     longer tied to what the kernel wants.
MISLEADS fires on NO corpus here. Only a problem on glibc >= 2.34; on musl
     and older glibc these are still constants and the code is fine.
`p + n < p` -- an overflow check the compiler deletes

ANSWERS a check that looks defensive and is not one.
ACT pointer addition that overflows is undefined behaviour, so the compiler
     folds `p + n < p` to false. Compare on integers:
     `(uintptr_t)p + n < (uintptr_t)p`. Detect with
     -fsanitize=pointer-overflow, which is opt-in -- hence this rule.
MISLEADS the pattern is matched textually, so a genuine comparison of two
     unrelated pointers that happen to share a name is listed. Fires on no
     corpus here, and is kept precisely because the compiler silently
     removes the check rather than warning about it.
calloc's arguments are the wrong way round

ANSWERS an allocation that is the wrong size and looks deliberate.
ACT calloc(count, size). A sizeof in the FIRST argument means the two are
     transposed: you asked for size*count elements of size bytes. GCC 14
     catches this with -Wcalloc-transposed-args, which is opt-in.
MISLEADS only the `calloc(sizeof(...)` spelling is detected; a named
     constant first argument that is really a size is invisible. Harmless
     when size == 1, which is common.
va_arg with an array type: undefined behaviour

ANSWERS a construct that cannot work at all.
ACT va_arg's type must be a promoted type the ABI can pass. An array type
     undergoes no promotion, so it never matches. Pass a pointer instead.
     Clang 20 diagnoses this as -Wvarargs; GCC does not by default.
MISLEADS fires on NO corpus in this tree -- it exists because the construct
     is unambiguous UB and the compiler only catches it with an opt-in flag.
A wall clock read where an elapsed time may be measured

ANSWERS where a clock adjustment, an NTP step or a DST change moves a timing.
ACT gettimeofday() and time() read the WALL clock, which steps backwards and
     forwards. For elapsed time use clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC), which
     cannot go backwards. Keep the wall clock only for timestamps.
MISLEADS this cannot tell measuring from timestamping -- and most wall-clock
     reads are legitimate timestamps that are correctly excluded by the
     `clock_gettime` test. A function that reads the clock to print a log
     line is listed. The filter is any gettimeofday/time/ftime/clock call
     with no CLOCK_MONOTONIC anywhere in the function, so the volume is high
     (143 rows across the corpora) by design: triage by fan_in.
An event wait that can return exactly one event per syscall

ANSWERS where the loop is syscall-bound instead of event-bound.
ACT pass a real array size. epoll_wait's maxevents of 1 -- or kevent's nevents
     of 1 -- means one syscall per event, which throws away the entire reason
     for using a poller instead of poll().
MISLEADS a maxevents of 1 is sometimes deliberate: nginx uses it in a probe
     that exists precisely to test one descriptor. Detected from the argument
     list only, so a variable that happens to hold 1 is invisible.
metricsCat: Read this first: where the call graph cannot see

ANSWERS how much of every other answer below is a lower bound.
ACT fnptr is the real blindness -- a callback table, a vtable-by-hand, a
     dispatch array. Reachability results for a module high on this list
     are floors, not facts. `via_macro` and `external` are NOT blindness:
     one is the preprocessor, the other is libc, and both are known.
MISLEADS this matches on NAME and body size only -- it never checks that
     the definitions sit behind a preprocessor conditional. Two
     same-named static functions in unrelated translation units, or one
     entry point implemented once per example module, look identical to
     a real backend pair. Confirm with grep -n '#if' on both files.
     fnptr also counts ordinary struct-member calls, and `unresolved`
     includes names from headers of libraries this run never walked into.
Where one fix multiplies: highest fan-in, ranked with complexity

ANSWERS which functions the rest of the tree leans on hardest.
ACT a win in a high-fan-in leaf pays back once per caller.
MISLEADS fan_in counts STATIC call sites, not dynamic frequency, and it
     cannot see a caller that reaches this through a function pointer.
Security review order: complexity x hazard x recursion

ANSWERS if you can only review N functions this week, which N.
ACT risk = 2*cyclo + cognitive + 5*nest + 10*memory + 8*io + 15*exec
     + integer + 2*alloc + 3*concurrency + 25 if recursive
     + 10 if it allocates and never frees.
MISLEADS it is a heuristic for ORDERING, not a list of findings.

ANSWERS what one call to this function really costs the allocator.
ACT `direct` counts allocation written in the body; `xalloc` walks the
     call graph and multiplies by static call sites.
MISLEADS the multiplier is STATIC call sites, not trip count, and the
     walk stops at depth 3 -- deeper allocation is not counted at all.
     Cycles are double-counted (a self-recursive wrapper's own mass is
     pushed back into it), so treat xalloc as an upper bound.
Cross-module call edges: where a seam would actually cut

ANSWERS how entangled the subsystems are.
ACT a heavy one-way edge is a real seam; a heavy pair is a cycle and the
     two modules are one module that has not admitted it.
MISLEADS counts DISTINCT caller/callee pairs, not runtime frequency, and
     misses every edge that goes through a callback.
Headers whose change rebuilds the most of the tree

ANSWERS which header is the build's bottleneck, transitively.
ACT split the widely-included header, or move the hot declarations into a
     narrow one. This is the cheapest build-time win in a C repo.
MISLEADS include depth is not compile cost, and a header included by
     everything but changed once a year costs nothing at all.
Loop depth >= 2: the O(n^k) candidates, with their per-iteration cost

ANSWERS where cost grows super-linearly in the input.
ACT check what bounds the INNER trip count. `divs` and `calls` are the
     two per-iteration costs people forget; a divide is ~20-40 cycles and
     a loop-invariant one should be a reciprocal multiply.
MISLEADS depth counts LEXICAL nesting, not asymptotics: an inner loop
     bounded by a constant is O(1).
Loops that CANNOT vectorise: a libm call in the body

ANSWERS which loops are categorically unvectorizable as written.
ACT a libm call in a loop body is a hard stop for the auto-vectoriser --
     it cannot prove the call is pure or replace it with a vector form.
     Use a vectorised math library, or a polynomial approximation.
MISLEADS it does not know the loop is hot, and -ffast-math plus a vector
     libm changes the answer entirely.

ANSWERS where the code already commits to a specific ISA.
ACT every intrinsic site needs a scalar fallback that is BUILT in CI, not
     merely present -- an unbuilt fallback is an unrun fallback.
MISLEADS a high intrinsic count is not a fast function, and `likely` hints
     are frequently wrong and never re-measured.
Byte-accurate layout: what reordering the fields would save

ANSWERS which structs waste memory on padding and exactly what the fix
     buys: `packed_sz` is the size with members declared widest-alignment
     first, `saves` the bytes back PER INSTANCE, and lines64_packed whether
     it then spans fewer cache lines.
ACT reorder to get packed_sz. No algorithm changes, and it compounds across
     every instance in every array. A row where lines64 drops is also one
     fewer cache miss per access.
MISLEADS LP64 model, exact=1 rows only: a struct holding a type this file
     does not define cannot be sized and is absent. A struct whose layout is
     an ABI -- written to disk, sent on the wire, shared with assembly --
     cannot be reordered at all, and one grouped for cache locality (hot
     fields first) may be right as it is: packed_sz is the floor, not a
     recommendation to ignore both.
Structs just over a 64-byte cache line

ANSWERS which hot objects need two cache lines where one would do.
ACT 65-128 bytes is the painful band: shrink below 64 and every access
     halves its memory traffic. Removing the padding is often enough.
MISLEADS a struct that is never hot does not care, and an object always
     touched in full needs both lines anyway.
Pointer-dense structs: each pointer field defeats the prefetcher

ANSWERS which structures drag a whole cache line to reach one field, and
     then send you somewhere else in memory to read it.
ACT candidates for splitting the hot fields into a parallel array (SoA).
MISLEADS TOP-LEVEL fields only -- union arms are alternatives, not extra
     fields -- and a node in a linked structure is pointer-dense by nature.
Stack bytes per function, and down the deepest call chain under it

ANSWERS which frames are large, and which entry points sit on top of the
     most stack: `chain_bytes` is this function's frame plus the heaviest
     acyclic path of callees below it, `chain_depth` how many frames that is.
ACT compare chain_bytes for every thread entry point against that thread's
     stack size. `biggest_local` names the usual culprit -- one buffer that
     belongs on the heap or in a static.
MISLEADS frame_bytes sums DECLARATIONS: sibling scopes share slots, so it
     overstates; `unsized` locals (a type this file does not define, a VLA)
     and saved registers are left out, so it understates. chain_bytes follows
     only calls the graph resolved -- nothing through a pointer -- and where
     `cyclic` is 1 a call back into the path was cut, so the true figure is
     unbounded and this one is a floor.
Pointer casts: where the type system was overruled

ANSWERS the places a wrong assumption becomes a memory bug.
ACT each cast is a claim the compiler cannot check. A cast next to I/O
     and shifting is where attacker-controlled bytes become a pointer.
MISLEADS the pattern counts some compound literals and some macro
     parameter lists as casts.
Function-like macros, by how much work they do

ANSWERS the code the call graph cannot see into at all.
ACT a heavily-used multi-line macro is a function that skipped review: no
     type checking, no breakpoint, no stack frame, and its cost is
     multiplied by every use site rather than shared.
MISLEADS `uses` counts sites where the name was called and no function of
     that name exists in the tree, so a macro shadowed by a real function
     somewhere reads as unused.

ANSWERS which regions a plain build silently omits.
ACT build each flag in CI, or the code inside it is unrun and unreviewed
     and will not compile the day someone needs it.
MISLEADS lists DIRECTIVES, not region sizes: one #ifdef can gate a
     thousand lines or a single semicolon.
One name, two definitions: which #if-selected backend is the STUB

ANSWERS where a compile-time alternative silently drops a feature.
ACT a body a fraction of its sibling's size is usually the stub, and the
     platform that selects it is the platform the feature does not work on.
MISLEADS a small body can be complete -- a one-line platform wrapper is
     the whole implementation on that platform.
static inline with real fan-in: zero self-time is not zero cost

ANSWERS which functions a sampling profiler CANNOT attribute cost to.
ACT never conclude one of these is cold from a flat profile -- its time
     is charged to whoever inlined it. `hidden` is fan_in * sloc, a rough
     measure of how much code the inliner is duplicating.
MISLEADS `static inline` is a request, not a guarantee, and a big one is
     often refused.
Complex functions with almost no comments

ANSWERS where the next reader has to reconstruct intent from the code,
     and where that reconstruction costs the most.
ACT a useful comment carries a CONSTRAINT or a non-obvious fact -- why
     the bound is 4096, which caller guarantees the pointer is non-NULL.
MISLEADS comment COUNT is not comment quality, and a genuinely obvious
     500-line switch needs no prose at all.
Build rules and object lists that enumerate their inputs by hand

ANSWERS which link targets name their objects individually -- both in a
     rule's prerequisites and in the OBJ= variable that feeds it, which is
     where a C project usually keeps the list.
ACT these are the lists a NEW CALL from a shared source silently breaks:
     the compile succeeds and the link fails naming a symbol nobody edited.
MISLEADS a hand-written list is perfectly correct until a dependency
     changes, so this is a fragility ranking, not a defect list. A probe
     snippet in a configure check looks the same and matters not at all.
How much of the tree this run actually read

ANSWERS whether any answer above is missing a chunk of the codebase.
ACT `errors` means braces or parentheses did not balance, so functions in
     that file may be merged, truncated or missed entirely. `unclosed` is
     an #if without an #endif. Both are worth reading before trusting a
     ranking that says a module is small.
MISLEADS a file with zero errors can still be mis-read: a macro that
     opens a brace and another that closes it balances perfectly and
     produces nonsense spans.

ANSWERS where a function has more than 3 goto statements, making control
     flow hard to follow and verify.
ACT restructure with structured control flow (if/else, while, break).
MISLEADS goto for cleanup-on-error (the only acceptable use in Linux kernel
     style) is correct but should be the only pattern.

ANSWERS where a function has max_nesting > 4, making it hard to verify.
ACT extract nested blocks into helper functions; use early returns.
MISLEADS C's max_nesting is +1 vs tree-sitter languages because it counts
     the function's own brace. Adjust thresholds accordingly.

ANSWERS where a function has more than 6 parameters.
ACT use a struct parameter.
MISLEADS a variadic function has n_params that does not count the ellipsis.
A function called from many different modules (shotgun surgery)

ANSWERS which functions are called from many distinct modules.
ACT consider splitting or stabilizing the contract.
MISLEADS a utility like memcpy or printf is called from everywhere.
Functions with many bare numeric literals (MISRA-C 7.4)

ANSWERS where a function has many magic numbers — bare numeric literals
     that are not 0 or 1 and have no named constant. Each is a
     maintenance burden.
ACT extract magic numbers into named constants or enums.
MISLEADS 0 and 1 are excluded by convention. Array indices and bit flags
     are sometimes clearer as literals.
Deepest resolved call chains: how far a change propagates downward

ANSWERS the functions with the widest downward exposure -- the count
     of DISTINCT functions each one can reach through resolved edges
     at any depth (precomputed in `reach.n_transitive_out`). Where
     blast-radius counts who can reach YOU (upward risk), this counts
     what you can REACH: the failure modes, allocation behaviour and
     locking you inherit every time you call down the stack.
ACT a wide fan under a request handler is where latency and error
     handling get lost; flatten, or make each level's contract
     explicit.
MISLEADS breadth, not depth: a function calling 30 helpers outranks a
     strict 12-level chain of 1-callee hops; calls through function
     pointers end the walk and undercount; a cycle member inherits its
     component's full reach.
Which modules own mutable file-scope state, and who writes it

ANSWERS the mutation map `race-surface` cannot draw: per module, the
    count of mutable file-scope objects against the number of
    functions that WRITE one of them in place. A module high on both
    columns is stateful by design and is where 'just add a feature'
    turns into 'understand six globals first'.
ACT the fix is architectural: group the globals into one context
    struct passed explicitly, so ownership shows up in signatures.
MISLEADS same-file references only (extern-through-header use is
    invisible), and a write counted here can be an initializer run
    once at startup -- volume of writes is not volume of races.
Where failure handling dominates the code

ANSWERS the functions whose shape IS error handling: return paths vs
    distinct failure shapes (NULL / negative / zero), null checks, and
    gotos-to-cleanup. C has no stack unwinding, so this work is real
    code with real branch cost -- and its absence is a defect while
    its excess is unreadability. This metric measures the balance.
ACT a high ratio with FEW null checks is the dangerous corner:
    failure-shaped but not checking allocations. Start there.
MISLEADS ret_* counts are textual (`return NULL;` exactly); a returned
    error ENUM or errno expression counts as ret_val, so a
    consistently-error-coded module looks value-returning; goto here
    includes non-cleanup uses.
Every allocation site, grouped by size-expression shape

ANSWERS the tree's actual allocation habits: raw byte counts vs
    sizeof-multiplied element counts vs bare constants, per allocator.
    The sizeof share is the single best proxy for allocation-safety
    discipline, and it is comparable across projects.
ACT read the shape mix before trusting any single leak query: a tree
    that allocates mostly through wrappers needs wrapper-level review,
    not site-level.
MISLEADS project allocator wrappers are invisible unless they call
    malloc/calloc/realloc directly IN THE BODY (they usually do, which
    is why the fn column matters); alloca rows are stack allocations
    and do not leak -- they exhaust the stack instead.
The heaviest memcpy-family users, with their copy-site inventory

ANSWERS which functions move the most bytes-by-call-count: the
    memcpy/memmove/strcpy/strcat/sprintf load ranked per function.
    Copy count is the cheapest available proxy for memory-bandwidth
    pressure, and these functions are also where a wrong length
    argument does the most damage.
ACT for the top rows ask the only two questions that matter: could
    this copy be a pointer swap, and is the length derived from input?
MISLEADS call COUNT, not bytes moved -- one memcpy of 4 KB outranks
    nothing here if the rest are 8-byte struct copies; copies inside
    loops multiply beyond what the count shows (join nested-loops for
    that).
Macro definitions ranked by transitive use weight

ANSWERS the preprocessor's real API surface: function-like macros
    weighted by use sites AND by body size -- n_uses * body_len is the
    amount of source the reader must simulate to understand one macro
    call. macro-machinery ranks by uses alone; this adds the cost side.
ACT the top rows are conversion candidates: a static inline function
    gives type checking and debuggability at identical runtime cost.
MISLEADS n_uses counts CALL-SHAPED uses only (name followed by '(');
    object-like macros used as constants show zero uses here, and a
    macro shadowed by a same-named function anywhere in the tree
    loses all its uses to that function.
Structs most exposed to layout change, weighted by field volatility

ANSWERS the structs whose byte layout carries the most cross-file
    weight: exact-sized, pointer-bearing, and defined in headers other
    files include. Reordering ONE field of these changes offsets in
    every consumer -- the ABI-compat question struct-padding answers
    for waste, answered here for RISK.
ACT pin the hot ones with _Static_assert(sizeof(struct x) == N) so a
    layout change fails the build instead of the customer.
MISLEADS header-defined structs only (a .c-local struct cannot leak
    its layout); usage is inferred from include edges, so a widely
    included header whose struct nobody instantiates still tops the
    list; exact=1 rows only.

ANSWERS where the code says out loud that it is not finished.
ACT read the SAFETY and UNSAFE markers first: those are usually a real
     invariant stated in prose because C cannot state it in types.
MISLEADS a marker is a comment, not a defect, and NOTE dominates every real
     codebase. The `markers` table has been populated since the base schema and
     nothing read it until now, so no convention about it has been established.
Functions with an identical size-and-shape fingerprint

ANSWERS where the same shape of code appears more than once.
ACT a fingerprint match is a place to LOOK, not proof of a copy. Read two rows
     before extracting anything.
MISLEADS the fingerprint is (sloc, cyclomatic, n_params, n_calls). Two entirely
     different functions can share it, and a genuine copy that gained one
     statement will not. `duplicated_sloc` is an upper bound on what could be
     removed and is usually far larger than what should be.
Same-typed pointer parameters with no restrict anywhere

ANSWERS where the compiler must assume two parameters overlap.
ACT add `restrict` where they genuinely cannot overlap and the reloads go away.
     Verify first: CERT EXP43-C -- an incorrect restrict is undefined behaviour.
MISLEADS "same type" is textual on the parameter type string, so two pointers
     to different structs that happen to share a spelling get paired, while a
     `void *` next to anything does not. Loop depth is the proxy for whether it
     matters: without a loop there is nothing to reload.

ANSWERS where to start when the answer has to be a file, not a function.
ACT `risk_per_100_sloc` normalises for size: a big file is not automatically a
     bad one, but a small file with a high density is.
MISLEADS risk is the C-weighted formula (memory, I/O, exec, recursion), so a
     file full of careful string handling ranks high without being unsafe.
The tree's real public interface, ranked by dependents

ANSWERS which functions are actually an API: defined in a .c, prototyped in a .h.
ACT these are the ones a signature change breaks across translation units, and
     the ones that need a written contract. `documented=0` on a high fan_in row
     is the shortest path to a better codebase.
MISLEADS `declared_in` counts prototype rows anywhere in the tree, so a name
     declared in several headers counts all of them. Inline functions in headers
     are excluded by construction, which is where much of a modern C API lives.
Function-like macros ranked by how much work they do

ANSWERS the macros whose expansion is doing real work in this tree.
ACT a macro used a thousand times is a function that cannot be stepped into,
     type-checked, or profiled. `do_while=0` on a multi-statement macro is the
     one to fix first.
MISLEADS `n_uses` counts calls resolved to this macro by NAME, so a macro
     invoked from inside another macro is attributed to the outer one. do_while
     is a substring test on the body, not a parse.
Locals declared without an initialiser, by function

ANSWERS the surface for EXP33-C: an uninitialised read.
ACT a local declared without an init is only a bug if it is READ before it is
     written, which this cannot prove. Ranked by count so the largest surfaces
     come first.
MISLEADS the dominant false positive is a variable assigned on all paths
     immediately after its declaration -- extremely common and entirely correct.
Each lock, by how much code runs while it is held

ANSWERS which lock is the actual contention point.
ACT a lock's cost is not how often it is acquired, it is how much work sits
     underneath: cyclo_under_lock and io_under_lock are the columns that predict
     stalls. Splitting a hot lock beats optimising what is under it.
MISLEADS attributed per FUNCTION that acquires the lock, not per critical
     section -- so everything in that function counts as "under the lock",
     including code that runs before the acquire. Only lock-shaped identifier
     names are recorded, so a lock held in a variable is invisible.
Typedefs whose underlying type is a pointer or an array

ANSWERS where the `*` is invisible at every use site.
ACT the reader cannot tell whether `Foo x` is one word or a thousand, whether
     `x = y` aliases or copies, or whether `sizeof x` is the pointer or the
     buffer. Naming it `FooPtr` is the cheap fix.
MISLEADS matched on the presence of `*` or `[` in the declared type text, so a
     typedef of a function pointer and a typedef of a struct that CONTAINS a
     pointer are both listed; only the first is the readability problem.
static inline bodies living in a header

ANSWERS code that is compiled once per including translation unit.
ACT `times_included` is the multiplier. These functions never appear in a
     profile under their own name and their cost is paid once per includer.
MISLEADS a header with none is absent from this list, not clean -- this is a
     presence ranking. `total_fan_in` sums the fan_in of the inlines, so a
     header with one heavily-used inline outranks one with thirty unused ones,
     which is the right order for build time and the wrong one for review.
Modules that cannot agree how to report failure

ANSWERS where a caller has to know the callee before it can check the result.
ACT pick one convention per module and write it down. `pct_mixed` is the share
     of that module's functions that use more than one shape.
MISLEADS computed over functions with at least one return, and the three shapes
     are NULL, a negative literal and a zero literal. Returning 0 for success AND
     0 as a legitimate value is the worst case of all and is invisible. Modules
     with fewer than 8 functions are excluded.
extern declarations sitting in a .c instead of a header

ANSWERS where a symbol's declaration is repeated per translation unit.
ACT move it to the header that owns the module, so the compiler can check every
     declaration against every other one.
MISLEADS `also_in_a_header` counts how many of this file's extern names ALSO
     appear in some header anywhere -- not necessarily one this file includes. A
     high number usually means the declaration is simply duplicated, which is
     still the problem.
Every function that touches epoll, io_uring or kqueue, with its flag profile

ANSWERS which functions own the event loop, and what contract each one has
     taken on -- edge or level, oneshot or not, errors watched or not.
ACT read this before any of the event-loop queries: it is the same columns
     unfiltered, so a row here that no query flags is a loop that is probably
     correct, and a row that several queries flag is where to start.
MISLEADS all counts are per FUNCTION. A project with one central dispatcher
     shows one row and looks simple; a project that inlines its loop shows
     dozens and does not necessarily have more problems.
The blocking wait loops, ranked by complexity

ANSWERS which event loop is the one worth understanding.
ACT a loop's cost is not the wait, it is everything under it. The per-loop
     columns -- calls, I/O and branches inside the loop body -- say whether
     the loop is a dispatcher or accidentally a worker.
MISLEADS 'loop' here means the function that calls the wait primitive, and
     the loop-body metrics cover every loop in that function, not only the
     event loop. Cyclomatic complexity ranks big dispatch switches highly,
     which is often the correct shape for one.
Per module: which of the three APIs, and how much of each contract is met

ANSWERS where the event-loop code lives and how disciplined it is.
ACT the six right-hand columns are the same predicates the event-loop
     queries use, counted instead of listed: eintr_blind, et_unprepared and
     leaks_instance are the rows those queries would return, so this is the
     denominator they lack.
MISLEADS every count is per FUNCTION, so a project with one central
     dispatcher shows a single dense row while a project that inlines its
     loop shows many sparse ones with the same total defects. Modules are
     two path components, so cross-directory loops are split.
Which toolchain namespaces each file uses, and how heavily

ANSWERS where the API surface of this codebase actually is.
ACT read this before any other rule in the pack: it is the denominator the
     per-rule queries lack. A file leaning hard on string.h deserves the
     string rules first.
MISLEADS grouped per FILE, so a project with one central wrapper file shows
     a single dense row while a project that calls libc everywhere shows many
     sparse ones with the same total. Namespaces are assigned by first match
     in sorted order, so a function declared by two headers is counted once.
Per file: how much of the API surface is used without its guard

ANSWERS which files are careless, not which individual calls are wrong.
ACT the five right-hand columns are the same predicates the per-rule queries
     use, counted instead of listed. Rank by the column that matters for the
     file's namespace mix.
MISLEADS every count is per FUNCTION and every guard test is function-wide,
     so a file with one careful helper and twenty careless callers scores
     badly for the right reason and a file with one careful helper and no
     callers scores perfectly for the wrong one. This is a triage ranking,
     not a defect count.
dynQueries: Transitive closure: every function attacker bytes can reach

ANSWERS the real attack surface: not just the functions that CALL read/
     recv, but everything downstream of them through resolved edges.
ACT this is the ranking to review before shipping a parser -- a bounds
     bug in any row here is a reachable memory-safety bug. The fuzz
     targets must cover the files named in this list (fuzz_parsers,
     fuzz_stdlib exist because of it).
MISLEADS fnptr edges are invisible: the aio/reactor dispatch and every
     JS_CFUNC-registered native are reached through function pointers,
     so this is a FLOOR, not the frontier. Compare against
     graph-blindspots before budgeting from it.
JSValue refcount drift: more JS_New*/JS_DupValue than JS_FreeValue

ANSWERS the CLAUDE.md law -- 'every value from an API call is owned; free
     once on every path' -- as a measurement, not a habit. Positive drift
     with early returns and a non-JSValue return type is the leak shape:
     a value created and then abandoned on an error path.
ACT a function that RETURNS a JSValue is exempt by design (the caller
     owns it now); a void/int function with drift > 0 and returns > 1
     needs a free on the paths that do not hand the value out.
MISLEADS counts are per function, not per path: a function that creates
     two values and frees one on every path can show 0 drift and still
     leak. Cross-check each row against its return statements.
More JS_FreeValue than JS_New*/JS_DupValue: double-free risk

ANSWERS the mirror of refcount-leak-shape: a function that frees more
     than it demonstrably creates inside itself. Two honest causes: the
     value was created OUTSIDE (caller-owned, must not free at all) or
     the creator is behind a macro the text pass cannot see.
ACT for each row: read the ownership comment. A negative drift on a
     function that also creates the value on one path is the double-
     free shape.
MISLEADS JS_FreeValueRT vs JS_FreeValue are both counted; a function
     freeing a borrowed JSValueConst is exactly the bug this exists to
     find, so treat every negative row as a review item.

ANSWERS where a peer-supplied key can retarget a prototype: JS_SetProperty
     and JS_SetPropertyStr walk the prototype chain, so a key of
     '__proto__' re-points the object. The repo rule is DEFINE for every
     decoded/mapped key. The on_frontier column comes from the taint
     closure; fnptr blindness undercounts it (registered natives are
     invisible), so 0 does not clear a row.
ACT walk the rows with the most calls first; a Set with a key built
     from input bytes (JSON keys, header names, map entries) must be
     JS_DefinePropertyValue. Internal fixed keys (error objects, option
     structs) are fine with Set.
MISLEADS the pass counts names, not arguments: a SetPropertyStr with a
     string LITERAL argument is a false positive for the prototype
     attack but still worth the walk (a later edit may hoist the key).
JSValue-returning functions with several returns and NO JS_Throw

ANSWERS where an error path returns a non-exception value: a native
     method that returns JS_UNDEFINED on failure instead of throwing
     reads as success to the caller and silently drops the failure.
ACT read the return statements; every failure path should throw a named
     error (the repo's distinct-refusal rule), never return quietly.
MISLEADS many honest functions return JS_EXCEPTION after a nested call
     already threw, with no JS_Throw of their own -- the count can be
     zero while every path is correct.
Mutable file-scope state: lazily-initialised statics and shared globals

ANSWERS the data-race class the codebase has hit before: a non-const
     static without an initialiser is a lazily-initialised static, and
     that is a data race even when every thread writes identical bytes.
     A non-static mutable global is shared state with no owner.
ACT prefer a compile-time const table; where a runtime probe is genuinely
     required, make the flag atomic.
MISLEADS a global only ever touched before thread creation is fine -- the
     scanner cannot see WHEN the write happens.

ANSWERS which modules cannot be reasoned about in isolation because
     each reaches the other through resolved calls. A module dependency
     cycle is the one smell that blocks architectural reasoning outright.
ACT break the most-loaded edge of the cycle (the pair with the highest
     out/in counts); a k-cycle of three shows as three rows here.
MISLEADS pairs are transitive, not direct: A->B->C->A reports (A,B),
     (A,C), (B,C). Each pair still names a real circular dependency.
     fnptr edges are invisible, so dispatch-table back-edges do not show.
Functions whose cross-module calls dominate their own-module calls

ANSWERS misplaced helpers: a function that calls into ONE foreign module
     far more than into its own is implemented on the wrong side of the
     boundary (the JDeodorant move-method shape).
ACT move the function into the envied module, or move the missing helper
     into the envious one; rank by cross_edges.
MISLEADS header-only helpers and shared utility modules (dyna-nat, cutils)
     are called by design; a function that envies a utility module is fine.
     Only module pairs that carry real domain logic are findings.
Callees with fan-in spread over the most files

ANSWERS the functions whose signature or contract change ripples into the
     most translation units: the static proxy for shotgun surgery.
ACT wrap in an accessor or push into the owning module BEFORE the next
     contract change; each row is a change-amplifier.
MISLEADS fan-in breadth is not churn: a stable, never-changing helper
     with 20 call sites is a good abstraction, not a smell. Judge by
     whether the contract is still evolving (markers nearby).
Huge AND complex AND central: the waiver-audit list

ANSWERS which functions are simultaneously large, deep and depended-upon.
     The repo rule: some functions are CORRECTLY enormous (a bytecode
     dispatch loop, GC machinery); everything else is an Extract-Function
     target, and the test is whether a sub-pass extracts without an asm diff.
ACT exempt the dispatch loops BY NAME, then rank the rest by cyclomatic
     x sloc and decompose.
MISLEADS a 500-line switch is often fine; a 300-line if-chain is not. The
     scanner cannot tell them apart -- n_switch is the discriminator.
Exported one-line forwarders called by many

ANSWERS pure pass-throughs on the API surface: short, trivial, widely
     called, and forwarding to exactly one callee.
ACT public ABI wrappers (JS_* forwarding to static internals) are
     intentional middle men and exempt BY DESIGN; the finding is only
     actionable when caller and callee share a module -- then the wrapper
     adds a hop without a boundary.
MISLEADS a wrapper that adds a check, a conversion or a log line is not
     a middle man; this list over-includes on purpose.
Non-static functions nothing in the tree references

ANSWERS the exported surface with no internal caller, no address taken,
     and no transitive caller: either JS-facing only (registered through
     JS_CFUNC_DEF lists the scanner cannot see) or genuinely dead.
ACT one grep of the registration tables per row settles it; dead rows are
     free untrusted-surface removal.
MISLEADS JS-facing natives are the expected majority -- the query exists
     to make the few non-registered rows findable.
Cross-module function pairs sharing the most callees

ANSWERS implicit coupling: two functions in different modules that call
     the same set of helpers change together when any of those helpers
     changes contract -- invisible in the module graph, visible in the
     call graph (the static proxy for logical coupling).
ACT pairs that hand-roll the same call sequence (JS_NewObject + SetProperty
     runs) are both a duplication and a cascade risk: extract the shared
     helper once.
MISLEADS shared UTILITY callees (memcpy, JS_FreeValue) create spurious pairs;
     require shared >= 4 so one common helper does not read as coupling.
Martin's instability I and distance D per module

ANSWERS which modules are stable (I~0: everyone depends on them) and which
     are unstable (I~1: they depend on everyone). With no abstract types
     in C, D = |1 - I|: the D~0.5 band is the danger zone -- a module with
     heavy in- AND out-edges is the change-preventer hub.
ACT I=0 with D=1 (the core runtime) means every change to it is shotgun
     surgery; its only relief is an interface boundary (fnptr table). D~0.5
     modules need a split, not more edits.
MISLEADS edge counts are static call sites; a module reached only through
     function pointers reads stabler than it is.
TODO/FIXME/HACK density per module: where the rot lives

ANSWERS which modules accumulate the deferred-work markers; density is
     the honest 'this is not finished' signal, and it concentrates where
     the risky parsers live.
ACT rank by markers BEFORE starting new work in a module: the existing
     debt is part of the effort estimate.
MISLEADS a stale marker stays forever; density alone does not say how old
     the debt is.
JS_ToCString/JS_ToCStringLen without matching JS_FreeCString on exit

ANSWERS where C string conversion buffers allocated by the engine
     are leaked on early return paths or missing cleanup. In QuickJS,
     every `JS_ToCString*` MUST be paired with `JS_FreeCString`.
ACT audit the non-paired return paths; ensure `JS_FreeCString` is
     invoked before every return or error exit, or the pointer is
     explicitly passed to an owned out-parameter (e.g. `powned`).
MISLEADS functions that return `const char *` or hand ownership to an
     out-parameter (e.g. `dyn_crypto_data`) show a positive difference
     by design. Check whether the pointer escapes.
JS_NewAtom* calls with fewer JS_FreeAtom releases

ANSWERS functions that allocate runtime atom table entries without
     releasing them. Atoms are reference-counted in QuickJS and
     leaked atoms stay permanently in the runtime atom table.
ACT ensure every `JS_NewAtom*` has a corresponding `JS_FreeAtom` on
     error paths, or is passed to an API function that adopts/defines
     the property.
MISLEADS atoms passed to property lookup/definition APIs that consume
     or store them internally may not need local `JS_FreeAtom`.

ANSWERS functions calling `JS_GetPropertyNames` or `JS_GetOwnPropertyNames`
     that fail to call `JS_FreePropertyEnum`. Calling raw `js_free` on
     the `JSPropertyEnum` array frees the array buffer but LEAKS all
     contained `JSAtom` entries.
ACT replace manual `free`/`js_free` with `JS_FreePropertyEnum(ctx, tab, ntab)`
     on all error and success exit paths.
MISLEADS functions that manually loop over `tab[i].atom` with `JS_FreeAtom`
     before calling `js_free` will appear here; prefer `JS_FreePropertyEnum`.
JS_Call / JS_Eval invocations without JS_IsException check

ANSWERS C functions executing JavaScript code (`JS_Call`, `JS_Eval`)
     that never check if the execution raised a pending JS exception.
     Unhandled exceptions stay on the JSContext and corrupt subsequent
     operations.
ACT check `if (JS_IsException(res))` immediately after the call and
     either handle or propagate it to the caller.
MISLEADS fire-and-forget logging or cleanup callbacks that explicitly
     clear exceptions via other helpers.
JS_GetOpaque callers without error checking or JS_Throw

ANSWERS functions calling `JS_GetOpaque` (which returns NULL without
     throwing on class mismatch) and not invoking any `JS_Throw*`.
     Dereferencing the returned pointer directly causes a NULL crash.
ACT use `JS_GetOpaque2` (which throws a TypeError on mismatch) or
     check `if (!ptr) return -1;` before dereferencing struct fields.
MISLEADS helper functions whose caller already validated the class ID.
Near-duplicate functions across different files (structural clones)

ANSWERS pairs of functions across different files with identical
     sloc, cyclomatic complexity, parameter count, and branch count:
     the static proxy for copy-paste code drift.
ACT factor the duplicated logic into a shared helper in `dyna-nat.h`
     or `cutils.h`.
MISLEADS multi-architecture SIMD kernel variants (SSE4.2 vs NEON vs
     AVX2) intentionally share exact structural signatures by design.
Functions with deep nesting (depth >= 5) or high branch count (>= 20)

ANSWERS control-flow hotspots that are hard to read and test.
ACT apply early returns, guard clauses, or extract inner loop bodies;
     for parsing state machines, evaluate table-driven dispatch (BOSCC).
MISLEADS complex tokenizer/parser switch cases may legitimately have
     many branches; check `n_switch` vs `max_nesting`.
Functions with high local variable count (>= 15) and multiple sizeofs

ANSWERS functions with heavy stack footprints from many local variables
     and local buffers, risking stack overflow in recursive loops or
     constrained thread stacks.
ACT move large stack buffers into heap scratch structures or arena
     allocators; reduce scope of temporary locals.
MISLEADS compiler register allocation can optimize non-aliased scalar
     locals into registers; arrays and structs are the real risk.
dynMetrics:
ANSWERS where the attack surface concentrates by module: functions
     reachable from io, with memory/alloc hazard counts and the fnptr
     blindness that makes every number a floor.
ACT budget security review by frontier_fns, then by mem+alloc; every
     parser module should appear here and its fuzz target should exist.
MISLEADS io roots only count RAW descriptor calls in the module's own
     functions -- a parser fed by a caller's read is reached through the
     graph, so it IS counted here, but its io column stays 0.
Per-module JS API call density: who owns the runtime boundary

ANSWERS which modules are the heaviest consumers of the JS runtime API
     (JS_New*/SetProperty/FreeValue family): the modules whose native
     methods do the most object plumbing are where the refcount and
     prototype-pollution bugs concentrate.
ACT cross-reference with refcount-leak-shape and define-vs-set per module.
MISLEADS counts include JS_Throw* (every native method throws); the
     ranking still holds because error paths are where the work is.
Per-module refactoring hotspots (god functions, deep nesting, complexity)

ANSWERS which modules have the highest concentration of complex,
     deeply nested, and oversized functions that need decomposition.
ACT prioritize refactoring sprints by god_fns count and total_cyclo.
MISLEADS core interpreter modules legitimately have high complexity.

ANSWERS which modules contain the most duplicate function structures
     that could be consolidated into common utility helpers.
ACT extract shared patterns into `dyna-nat.h` or module-internal helpers.
MISLEADS SIMD architecture variants naturally appear as clone pairs.
dynShapeQueries: An engine call with no hop-back macro, in a file that offloads to a thread

ANSWERS where code that may run on a compute thread can reach the JS
     runtime. A file calling dyn_fiber_offload must redefine every engine
     call it uses as a macro that returns to the JS thread first
     (#define JS_X(...) (dyn_fiber_onjs(), JS_X(__VA_ARGS__))); this lists
     the context-taking calls with no such macro.
ACT add the macro beside the others, never a manual hop at the call site.
MISLEADS module registration (JS_NewCModule and friends) runs once at
     import and is exempt by name; a call through a function pointer is
     invisible here.
A JS_Call result is freed with no exception handling in the function

ANSWERS where a handler that throws is silently lost AND leaves its
     exception pending on the context: JS_FreeValue of JS_EXCEPTION frees
     nothing, so the error is still there for the next unrelated caller of
     JS_GetException. Shipped once: DNSResolver.query callbacks were dropped
     this way while TCP/UDP handlers were counted and cleared.
ACT hand the result to the module's accounting (dyn_net_handler_result,
     dyn_call_drop) or test JS_IsException and clear with JS_GetException.
MISLEADS a promise's own resolve/reject function cannot throw; rows where
     every dropped call is one have resolver_only = 1 and sort last. The
     callee column is the text of the second argument, nothing more.
x - round_fn(...) * y: exact only where the compiler fuses it

ANSWERS where a result is correct on arm64 and wrong on x86-64. A
     remainder written as x - floor(x / y) * y is exact only when the
     multiply and subtract are ONE fused operation; arm64 compilers contract
     it into an FMA, baseline x86-64 has none and rounds twice. Shipped once:
     mathx.mod(1e17, 3) returned the wrong remainder on x86.
ACT write the fused operation explicitly -- fma(-q, y, x) -- or use fmod.
     Prove it natively with ./build.sh build CONFIG_FP_NOCONTRACT=y.
MISLEADS a bucket or grid edge (floor(t / w) * w with no exactness claim)
     has the shape and is only platform-divergent in the last ulp, not
     wrong. has_fma_call = 1 means the function already asks for fusion
     somewhere, not necessarily at this site.

ANSWERS which ring setups bypass the memlock step-down. Ring memory is
     charged against RLIMIT_MEMLOCK and a closed ring's charge comes back
     asynchronously; a fixed 8192-entry ring failed with ENOMEM after ten
     reactors at the common 8 MiB limit. dyn_uring_ring_open halves the ring
     on ENOMEM and waits at the floor.
ACT route the setup through dyn_uring_ring_open.
MISLEADS a short-lived probe ring of a few entries (dyna-uring.c's disk
     queue) is small enough not to matter; it still appears.
dyn_net_reactor_acquire without the shared failure error

ANSWERS which callers report a missing reactor in their own words. Every
     class that needs the reactor must fail the same way and say why
     (io_uring unavailable or denied); dyn_net_throw_no_reactor is that one
     sentence.
ACT replace the local JS_Throw with dyn_net_throw_no_reactor(ctx, who).
MISLEADS a caller that cannot throw (a C-only path returning NULL) is
     listed and is fine.
Prototype-walking set whose KEY is not a literal

ANSWERS the real prototype-pollution candidates. JS_SetProperty and
     JS_SetPropertyStr walk the prototype chain, so a peer-chosen key of
     __proto__ retargets the object; define-vs-set lists every caller, this
     lists only the calls whose key is computed.
ACT a key that comes from input -- a JSON member, a header name, a column
     -- must be written with JS_DefinePropertyValue*.
MISLEADS a key held in a local that was itself assigned a literal reads as
     dynamic. on_frontier comes from the io taint closure, which cannot see
     calls through a function pointer: 0 does not clear a row.
JS_NewTypedArray over a BUFFER with fewer than three arguments

ANSWERS a view that is silently EMPTY. One argument that is an array
     buffer builds a length-0 view over it; a handler handed that loops
     zero times and reports success.
ACT pass (buffer, byteOffset, length).
MISLEADS one argument that is a LENGTH is the ordinary allocation and is
     not listed. The buffer test is by name (buf, ab, buffer) or by an
     assignment from JS_NewArrayBuffer* in the same function, so a buffer
     passed in under another name is missed.
A sleep or synchronous resolver call in reactor code

ANSWERS where one connection's wait becomes every connection's wait.
ACT move the wait onto a timer, the lookup onto the pool.
MISLEADS a deliberate bounded pause on a failure path (the ring-open
     reclaim wait) and code that runs on a pool thread rather than the
     reactor both appear; the file filter is by name, not by thread.
fsync with no F_FULLFSYNC in the function

ANSWERS which durability claims hold on Linux only. On Darwin fsync
     returns when the data reaches the drive, not when the drive has
     committed it; F_FULLFSYNC is the durable form.
ACT fcntl(fd, F_FULLFSYNC) first, plain fsync as the ENOTSUP fallback.
MISLEADS a flush that is advisory by design.
strtod / atof / scanf %f: the radix character is the locale's

ANSWERS where a wire or file format is parsed with a function that reads
     LC_NUMERIC and also accepts hex floats, leading space and partial
     input. One setlocale call elsewhere and every float loses its fraction.
ACT hand-roll the grammar the format states.
MISLEADS parsing a number a USER typed in their own locale is correct with
     strtod. on_frontier is the io taint closure (a floor).
(void) on a call that arms, registers or submits

ANSWERS where 'did the thing I depend on get set up' is thrown away. A
     discarded timer or watcher registration makes every hook behind it
     silent, and the caller's status check passes because it was never
     wired to this.
ACT propagate the failure, or refuse the operation.
MISLEADS a best-effort re-arm on a path that is already failing.
